groups.note: All come from ところ (所, “place”) — placing an event at a certain point in time

items.diff: たところだ ends the sentence and means “just did”; たところで sits mid-sentence and means “even if… (it's no use)”.

this.tr: The train has just left.

that.tr: Even if I run now, I won't make it in time.

items.explain: Look at what follows ところ: if it's 「だ」 and the sentence ends → “just did”; if it's 「で」 and another clause follows, usually a negative or “it's no use” result → “even if…”.

items.diff: たところだ says an action has “just finished”; たところ、 says “I did it, and as a result found…”.

this.tr: I've just sent an email to my teacher.

that.tr: I emailed my teacher, and got a reply right away.

items.explain: At the end of a sentence, 「たところだ」 only marks a point in time; mid-sentence, 「たところ、」 is always followed by a result (often an unexpected discovery), and the whole sentence is in the past tense. If something happens after 「たところ、」, it's the “result” use.

items.diff: ところだ only says what point in time you are at; ところに／へ says “right at that moment, someone or something came along”.

this.tr: I'm just about to go out.

that.tr: Just as I was about to go out, a friend came over.

items.explain: ところに／ところへ is always followed by someone or something that “bursts in” (友達が来た, 電話が鳴った), often disrupting your plans; ところだ only describes your own state, and the sentence ends there.

items.diff: ところだ is a real point in time; ところだった means “almost…”, but it didn't actually happen.

this.tr: I'm just about to arrive at the station.

that.tr: I very nearly missed the train.

items.explain: Look for words like 「もう少しで」「危うく」 and the past tense 「だった」: ところだった describes something that almost happened but didn't, often with relief or a sense of a close call; ところだ describes a real point in time right now.

groups.note: ところ ↔ どころ — they differ only by the voicing mark (dakuten)

items.diff: ところ means “just now”; どころか means “far from…, in fact / not even…”.

this.tr: I've just finished my homework.

that.tr: Far from finishing my homework, I haven't even started it.

items.explain: First check for the dakuten: ど ≠ と. Then look at the structure: before どころか comes an “expectation”, and after it a fact that is the complete opposite and even more extreme, so the sentence always contrasts two parts.

items.diff: たところだ means “just now”; どころではない means “in no position to… at all”.

this.tr: I've just finished work.

that.tr: I'm so busy with work that a trip is out of the question.

items.explain: どころではない usually follows a noun (旅行, 勉強), ends with the negative 「ではない」, and is often preceded by a reason (忙しくて); it has nothing to do with a point in time. If you see ど + a negative at the end, it isn't “just now”.

groups.note: Both mean “just (now)”

items.diff: たところ is objectively “this very moment”; たばかり is subjectively “not long ago”, and can even be used for something months ago.

this.tr: I've just arrived in Japan (this very moment).

that.tr: I only came to Japan last month.

wrong.why: A month has passed, so you can't use たところ

items.explain: Look at the time word: 「今」 — the action ended right before speaking → たところ; 「先月」 — some time has objectively passed, but the speaker feels it was “not long ago” → only たばかり works.

items.diff: たところだ ends the sentence and marks a point in time; たて modifies a noun, stressing “freshly made, brand-new”.

this.tr: The bread has just finished baking.

that.tr: I bought freshly baked bread.

items.explain: たて attaches to a verb's masu-stem (焼き + たて) and is used like an adjective: 「〜たての + noun」. It only works with a handful of verbs (焼きたて, できたて, 生まれたて); to say that something has just happened, use たところだ.

groups.note: Both come from ばかり — originally “only this much”

items.diff: ta-form + ばかり means “just did”; noun + ばかり means “nothing but, all”.

this.tr: I just bought this computer.

that.tr: This shop sells nothing but expensive things.

items.explain: It's the same ばかり, originally meaning “only this”. Look at what comes before it: a ta-form (買った) → “only this little time has passed” = just now; a noun (物) → “only this one kind” = nothing but.

items.diff: たばかり means “just finished doing”; てばかりいる means “always doing, doing nothing but”, often with a complaint.

this.tr: I just ate a little while ago.

that.tr: My little brother does nothing but play games every day.

items.explain: The only difference is た vs. て: た + ばかり is about a short time; て + ばかり + いる is about doing the same thing over and over, and the speaker is often unhappy about it. If you see 「ている」, it means “always”.

groups.note: たばかりだ ↔ たばかりに — they differ only in the last character

items.diff: たばかりだ means “just did”; たばかりに means “just because… (it led to a bad result)”.

this.tr: I've just come to Japan.

that.tr: Just because I said one thing too many, I made her angry.

items.explain: Both are 「た + ばかり」, differing only in the final 「だ」 or 「に」. たばかりに is always followed by a clause with a bad result (〜てしまった), meaning “it was only because of that small thing that…”, often with regret.

groups.note: Both mean “just (now)”

items.diff: たばかり is subjectively “not long ago”; たところだ is objectively “this very moment”.

this.tr: I only came to Japan last month.

that.tr: I've just arrived in Japan (this very moment).

wrong.why: A month has passed, so you can't use たところ

items.explain: Look at the time word: 「先月」 — some time has objectively passed, but the speaker feels it was “not long ago” → たばかり; 「今」 — the action ended right before speaking → both たところ and たばかり work, but たところ puts more stress on “at this very moment”.

items.diff: たばかり works with any verb; たて only attaches to a few verbs and stresses “freshly made, brand-new”.

this.tr: I lost the umbrella I just bought yesterday.

that.tr: Freshly baked bread is delicious.

items.explain: たて attaches directly to the masu-stem (焼き + たて) and is only used with a few words where “the thing made is still new”: 焼きたて, できたて, 生まれたて, 塗りたて. In every other case use たばかり, e.g. 「昨日買ったばかりの傘」.

groups.note: All come from よう (様) — “a certain state or way”

items.diff: ようになる is a change that happens naturally (“come to…”); ようにする is something you deliberately “make a point of doing”.

this.tr: Since my child was born, I've (without noticing) started getting up early.

that.tr: I make a point of getting up early for my health.

items.explain: Look at the first half marked with the dotted line: “since my child was born” is an outside cause, and getting up early is the result of changed circumstances → ようになる; “for my health” is your own goal, and getting up early is a habit you consciously keep → ようにする. Memory tip: なる = become, する = do.

items.title: 〜ように (purpose)
items.diff: ようになった is a result already achieved; ように is a goal not yet reached that you're still working toward.

this.tr: I practiced every day, so now I can read kanji.

that.tr: I practice every day so that I'll be able to read kanji.

items.explain: Both sentences are about the same thing, just seen from different points in time. Look at what follows ように: if the sentence ends right there → it has already happened (ようになった); if it goes on to say “what you're doing for it” → it's a goal (ように).

items.diff: ようになる means “a person has come to be able to / started to…”; ようになっている means “a machine or system is designed to…”.

this.tr: My child can now get dressed on their own.

that.tr: This door is designed to open automatically when someone approaches.

items.explain: Look at the subject: a person or animal → a change in ability or habit (ようになった); a machine, system or rule → a mechanism designed that way from the start (ようになっている), often together with 「〜と」. It isn't a “change” at all.

groups.note: Both express “change”, but are used differently

items.diff: Both mean “change”; the difference is what they attach to: verbs take ようになる; adjectives and nouns take くなる／になる.

this.tr: I can swim now.

that.tr: I've gotten good at swimming.

wrong.why: A verb can't attach directly to になる

items.explain: First check what kind of word comes before 「なる」: 泳げる is a verb → ようになる; 上手 is a na-adjective → になる (i-adjectives: 寒い → 寒くなる; nouns: 医者 → 医者になる). In English both are just “become / get…”, so learners easily write ✗泳げるになった.

items.diff: ようになる looks at the “end point” of a change (now you can); てくる looks at the “process” (it's changing bit by bit).

this.tr: After three months, I came to understand Japanese.

that.tr: Little by little, I've started to understand Japanese.

items.explain: Look at the time words: 「３か月で」 sets an end point and describes the new state once it's reached → ようになる; 「少しずつ」 describes the process of change, which is still going on up to now → てくる is common.

groups.note: All come from よう (様) — “a certain state or way”

items.diff: ようにする is something you deliberately “make a point of doing”; ようになる is a change that happens naturally (“come to…”).

this.tr: I make a point of getting up early for my health.

that.tr: Since my child was born, I've (without noticing) started getting up early.

items.explain: Look at the first half marked with the dotted line: “for my health” is your own goal, and getting up early is a habit you consciously keep → ようにする; “since my child was born” is an outside cause, and getting up early is the result of changed circumstances → ようになる. Memory tip: する = do, なる = become.

items.diff: ようにする is your own effort; ように言う is telling someone else to do it.

this.tr: I try to eat vegetables every day.

that.tr: My doctor told me to eat vegetables every day.

items.explain: Look at who made the request: a goal you set for yourself → ようにする; a request from a doctor, teacher or boss → ように言う／ように言われた, often with 「〜に」 before it marking who said it.

groups.note: Both relate to “planning or deciding to do something”

items.diff: ようにする means “try to, make an effort to”, with no guarantee you'll manage every time; ことにする means “decide to”, settled once and for all.

this.tr: I try not to eat sweets.

that.tr: I've decided to give up sweets starting today.

items.explain: Look at the adverbs: 「なるべく」「できるだけ」 often go with ようにする and show the direction of your effort; 「今日から」 with 「ことにした」 shows a decision made at a particular moment.

items.diff: ようにしている is an effort you're already keeping up; つもりだ is a plan in your head that hasn't started yet.

this.tr: I make a point of going to bed by 11 every night.

that.tr: I plan to start going to bed early next week.

items.explain: Look at the time: ようにしている describes a habit you're already doing and keeping up now; つもりだ describes a future plan, and whether it actually happens is still unknown.

groups.note: Both come from the appearance そう — “how something looks”

items.diff: そうだ means “looks like it's going to…”; そうになる means “almost…”, but it didn't actually happen.

this.tr: The sky is dark. It looks like it's going to rain.

that.tr: I slipped and almost fell.

items.explain: そうだ is a judgment based on what you see in front of you; そうになった is something that “was about to happen to you but in the end didn't”, and is almost always in the past tense 「なった」.

items.diff: そうだ means “looks like it will…”; そうもない means “doesn't look like it will…”.

this.tr: It looks like this work will be finished today.

that.tr: It doesn't look like this work will be finished today.

items.explain: The two sentences differ only in the final 「だ」 vs. 「もない」. The most natural way to negate appearance そうだ is to put the negative after そう: 終わりそうもない／終わりそうにない, meaning “there's no sign at all that it will…”.

groups.note: All mean “seems, looks like”

items.diff: そうだ predicts from how things look (it hasn't happened yet); ようだ infers from evidence (it has most likely already happened).

this.tr: The sky is dark. It looks like it's going to rain.

that.tr: The road is wet. It seems it has rained.

items.explain: Look at the clue in the first half: you see the state “the sky is dark” and predict what comes next → そうだ (attaches to the masu-stem: 降り + そう); you see the result “the road is wet” and infer what already happened → ようだ (attaches to the plain form: 降った + よう).

items.diff: そうだ (appearance) is what you see with your own eyes; らしい is usually information you heard or got indirectly.

this.tr: This cake looks delicious.

that.tr: According to my friend, the cakes at that shop are supposed to be delicious.

items.explain: Look at the source of the information: the cake is right in front of you → おいしそう; you only heard it from someone and haven't tried it → おいしいらしい. Also note how they attach: そうだ attaches to the stem (おいし + そう), らしい to the plain form (おいしい + らしい).

items.diff: Hearsay そうだ is ordinary reporting; とのことだ is more formal and is often used to pass on someone's message.

this.tr: According to the news, it will snow tomorrow.

that.tr: I have a message from the manager: the meeting starts at 3.

items.explain: Both can mean “I heard that…”, but とのこと is common at work and in letters, with a sense of “I'm passing this on for them”. Also note: hearsay そうだ attaches to the plain form (降る + そうだ); don't confuse it with appearance 降り + そうだ (“looks like it's going to rain”).

groups.note: Both come from よう (様) — “a certain state or way”

items.diff: ようだ is a judgment based on the evidence taken together; ように見える only says how something “looks on the outside”, which may not be true.

this.tr: The lights are off. It seems nobody's home.

that.tr: He looks angry, but he actually isn't.

items.explain: ように見える only describes how something “looks”, and is often followed by 「が、本当は……」, which overturns it; ようだ is the speaker's judgment after putting the clues together, and they basically believe it.

items.diff: ようだ (simile) is an ordinary comparison; かのようだ means “just as if…” about something you know isn't true, so the contrast is stronger.

this.tr: Her hands are as cold as ice.

that.tr: He's smiling as if nothing had happened.

items.explain: かのようだ follows a clause that “isn't actually true” (何もなかった), emphasizing the gap between appearance and reality; ordinary ようだ usually follows “noun + の” and is just a simple comparison.

groups.note: All mean “seems, looks like”

items.diff: ようだ infers from evidence (it has most likely already happened); そうだ predicts from how things look (it hasn't happened yet).

this.tr: The road is wet. It seems it has rained.

that.tr: The sky is dark. It looks like it's going to rain.

items.explain: Look at the clue in the first half: you see the result “the road is wet” and infer what already happened → ようだ (attaches to the plain form: 降った + よう); you see the state “the sky is dark” and predict what comes next → そうだ (attaches to the masu-stem: 降り + そう).

items.diff: ようだ is a judgment based on clues you perceive yourself; らしい is usually based on things you've heard, with a flavor of “reportedly”.

this.tr: I can hear something from the next room. Someone seems to be there.

that.tr: Rumor has it those two are getting married.

items.explain: Look at what the judgment is based on: direct clues you heard or saw yourself → ようだ／みたいだ; indirect information such as rumors or what others said → らしい. With らしい, the speaker sounds detached, as if not taking responsibility for the claim.

groups.note: Both come from はず (筈) — “by reason, logically”

items.diff: はずだ means “logically, it should be so”; はずがない means “logically, it can't possibly be so”.

this.tr: He's lived in Japan for ten years, so he should be able to speak Japanese.

that.tr: He's never studied it even once, so there's no way he can speak Japanese.

items.explain: Look at the reason given in the first half: if it supports the conclusion → はずだ; if it clearly can't lead to the conclusion → はずがない. Note that はずがない is a strong “absolutely impossible”, much stronger than 「話せないはずだ」 (“he shouldn't be able to speak it”).

groups.note: Both mean “judging by logic”

items.diff: はずだ is a logical guess made beforehand; わけだ is “no wonder, so that's why” said afterwards.

this.tr: I sent the package yesterday, so it should arrive tomorrow.

that.tr: Oh, you sent it yesterday? Then no wonder it's already here.

items.explain: はずだ is for guessing when you don't know the result yet; わけだ is for when you already know the result and, on learning the reason, think “that makes sense”. It's often preceded by 「それなら」「だから」「〜のか」.

items.diff: はずだ has objective grounds (logic); に違いない is a strong subjective conviction (a gut feeling).

this.tr: According to the schedule, the manager should be attending the 3 o'clock meeting.

that.tr: Judging by that smile, something good must have happened.

items.explain: Behind はずだ you can name concrete grounds (a schedule, a rule, a calculation); に違いない is the speaker's own strong feeling, and the grounds can be nothing more than an impression. That's why はずだ is more common when talking about work or in writing.

groups.note: All come from わけ (訳) — “reason, logic”

items.diff: わけだ means “no wonder, naturally”; わけがない means “there's no way”.

this.tr: He practices every day, so no wonder he's good.

that.tr: He's never practiced even once, so there's no way he's good.

items.explain: わけ = reason. わけだ: there's a reason, so “no wonder”; わけがない: there's no such reason at all, so “impossible”. Look at the first half: a solid reason is given → わけだ; the reason obviously doesn't hold → わけがない.

items.diff: わけだ draws the conclusion that logically follows; わけではない means “it's not that…”, a partial denial.

this.tr: Oh, you lived there for three years? No wonder you know Japan so well.

that.tr: I did live in Japan, but that doesn't mean I know it well.

items.explain: わけではない corrects an inference that seems “only natural”: lived in Japan ≠ necessarily knows Japan well. If you see 「けど」 or 「からといって」 earlier in the sentence, what follows is most likely わけではない.

items.diff: わけだ says “that's just how it logically is”; わけにはいかない says “I can't do that, for reasons of logic or responsibility”.

this.tr: Oh, he has an exam tomorrow? So that's why he isn't going out.

that.tr: I have an exam tomorrow, so I can't go out and play.

items.explain: The subject of わけにはいかない is usually the speaker, meaning “I'd like to, but because of responsibility, rules or obligations to others, I can't”; わけだ explains a known fact and has nothing to do with whether you “can or can't”.

groups.note: Both mean “judging by logic”

items.diff: わけだ is “no wonder, so that's why” said afterwards; はずだ is a logical guess made beforehand.

this.tr: Oh, you sent it yesterday? Then no wonder it's already here.

that.tr: I sent the package yesterday, so it should arrive tomorrow.

items.explain: わけだ is for when you already know the result and, on learning the reason, think “that makes sense”; it's often preceded by 「それなら」「だから」「〜のか」. はずだ is for guessing when you don't know the result yet.

groups.note: Both come from ため (為) — “purpose, cause”

items.diff: ために sits inside the sentence, right after the cause or purpose; そのため starts a sentence and refers back to the previous one.

this.tr: The trains stopped because of heavy snow.

that.tr: There was heavy snow last night. Because of that, the trains stopped.

items.explain: Same meaning, different position: ために comes right after the cause, all in one sentence; そのため is a standalone conjunction that needs a sentence before it, and 「その」 refers to what that sentence said.

groups.note: All mean “in order to” or “because”

items.title: 〜ように (purpose)
items.diff: ために follows actions you can control; ように follows states, such as potential or negative forms.

this.tr: I study every day in order to pass the N1.

that.tr: I study every day so that I can speak Japanese.

wrong.why: After a potential form, use ように

items.explain: Look at the verb before ため／ように: 「合格する」 is an action you decide to do → ために; potential forms, negative forms and things that happen on their own, like 「話せる」「忘れない」「見える」 → ように.

items.title: 〜から (reason)
items.diff: ために (cause) is more formal/written and is followed by an objective result that has already happened; から is more conversational and can be followed by invitations, requests or commands.

this.tr: The trains are delayed due to an accident.

that.tr: We're out of time, so let's hurry.

wrong.why: ために of cause can't be followed by an invitation or command

items.explain: Look at the second half: stating a result that has already happened, like a station announcement or the news → ために; your own invitation or request, like 「〜よう」「〜てください」 → only から (or ので) works.

items.title: 〜には (purpose)
items.diff: ために is followed by “what you do”; には is followed by “what's needed, what it takes”.

this.tr: I'm saving money to buy a house.

that.tr: To buy a house, you need a lot of money.

items.explain: Look at the second half: an action you're taking (貯金している) → ために; a need or evaluation such as 「必要だ」「〜がかかる」「〜がいい」 → には.

groups.note: All come from こと (事) — turning an action into the content of a decision

items.diff: ことにする is your own decision; ことになる is decided by others or by circumstances.

this.tr: After thinking it over myself, I decided to quit my job.

that.tr: On the company's orders, I'm being transferred to Osaka.

items.explain: Look at who made the decision: 「自分で考えて」 → ことにした; 「会社の命令で」 → ことになった. Also, Japanese speakers sometimes deliberately use ことになった for their own decisions, to sound modest and low-key.

items.diff: ことにした is a decision made at one moment; ことにしている is a personal rule kept up over a long time.

this.tr: Starting today, I've decided to go running every morning.

that.tr: For five years now, I've made a point of running every morning.

items.explain: Look at the time words: 「今日から」 marks the moment of deciding → ことにした; 「もう５年」「いつも」 show it's been kept up for a long time → ことにしている.

items.diff: ことにする is a personal decision; ことになっている is a rule, a system, or an arrangement settled in advance.

this.tr: I've decided not to look at my phone at night.

that.tr: In this dorm, you're not allowed to go out after 10 p.m.

items.explain: Look at where the decision comes from: something you set for yourself → ことにする／ことにした; the rules of a school, company or dorm, or an arrangement agreed on in advance → ことになっている.

groups.note: Both relate to “planning or deciding to do something”

items.diff: ことにした is the moment you make up your mind; つもりだ is a plan you've had in mind.

this.tr: I hesitated for a long time, but I've decided to study abroad.

that.tr: I plan to study abroad next year.

items.explain: ことにした often carries a sense of “finally deciding after hesitating” (迷ったけど, いろいろ考えて); つもりだ just states an intention without stressing the moment of decision, and you might not end up going.

items.diff: ことにする follows a verb; にする follows a noun and is often used to pick one of several options.

this.tr: I've decided to go to Okinawa for summer vacation.

that.tr: For my drink, I'll have coffee.

wrong.why: After a verb, you need 「こと」

items.explain: First check whether a verb or a noun comes before it: 行く (verb) → ことにする; コーヒー (noun) → にする. 「〜にします」 is most common when ordering food or choosing something.

groups.note: Both come from the i-adjective continuative form 「く」 — whose job is to “link to the next word”

items.diff: く directly modifies the following action (how it's done); く＋て first finishes describing one quality, then moves on.

this.tr: At this shop you can buy vegetables cheaply.

that.tr: The vegetables at this shop are cheap and fresh.

items.explain: Both are the continuative form 「く」 — look at what follows: a verb right after it (買える) → describes how the action is done; an added 「て」 followed by another quality (新しい) → lists the qualities side by side.

groups.note: Both come from the i-adjective continuative form 「く」 — whose job is to “link to the next word”

items.diff: くて＝く＋て: finish one quality, then continue; く directly modifies the following verb.

this.tr: This bread is cheap and tasty.

that.tr: I get up early every morning.

wrong.why: To modify the verb 「起きる」, use く

items.explain: Both are the continuative form 「く」 — look at what follows: an added 「て」 followed by another quality (おいしい) → lists them side by side; a verb right after it (起きる) → describes how the action is done.

groups.note: All can link two things: listing several qualities, or giving a reason

items.title: 〜から (reason)
items.diff: When くて gives a reason, only a naturally occurring result can follow; if a request or invitation follows, you must use から.

this.tr: It's so hot I can't sleep.

that.tr: It's hot, so please open the window.

wrong.why: くて can't be followed by a request or command

items.explain: Look at the second half: a result you can't control, like 「眠れない」 or 「困る」 → くて／で is fine; a request or intention, like 「〜てください」 or 「〜ましょう」 → only から (or ので) works.

items.diff: くて simply lists things flatly; し lists points one by one as reasons, implying “there's more”, and is often followed by a conclusion.

this.tr: This place is cheap and tasty.

that.tr: This place is cheap, and it's tasty, so I come here often.

items.explain: Look for a “so…” conclusion: if it only describes what something is like → くて; if several good points serve as reasons leading to a judgment like “so I come often” → し. They also attach differently: くて is a conjugated adjective, while し follows the plain form (安いし).

groups.note: Both come from あまり (余り) — originally “exceeding, excess”

items.diff: あまり＋negative means “not very…”; あまりに＋affirmative means “too…”.

this.tr: These clothes aren't very expensive.

that.tr: These clothes are too expensive — I can't buy them.

items.explain: Check whether the adjective after it is negative or affirmative: 「高くない」 → あまり＝not very; 「高くて買えない」 → あまりに＝excessively, often followed by a “so there's nothing I can do” result.

groups.note: All pair with a negative to say how much or how often something is “not” done

items.diff: あまり〜ない means “not very”, leaving some room; 全然〜ない means “not at all”.

this.tr: I don't drink much — just a little now and then.

that.tr: I don't drink at all — I can't have even a sip.

items.explain: Look at what's added afterwards: “I drink a little now and then” → あまり; “not even a sip…”, with no room at all → 全然.

items.diff: あまり can describe both degree and frequency; めったに only describes frequency — “rarely, seldom”.

this.tr: This apple isn't very sweet.

that.tr: My father rarely gets angry.

items.explain: Check whether it's about “how often” or “to what degree”: an action that seldom happens (怒らない、行かない) → both あまり and めったに work, with めったに being rarer; the degree of an adjective (甘くない、高くない) → only あまり.

groups.note: Both come from the copula 「です」 — でしょう＝です＋「う」, which expresses conjecture

items.diff: です states something for certain; でしょう is a guess — “probably”.

this.tr: Tomorrow is Sunday.

that.tr: It will probably rain tomorrow.

items.explain: Ask whether it's an established fact: something fixed on the calendar → です; things you can't be sure of yourself, like the weather or someone else's situation → でしょう, often used with 「たぶん」 or 「きっと」.

groups.note: Both come from だけ (丈) — expressing “a limit, only this much”

items.diff: だけ just limits the scope; だけで says “just this alone is enough to…”.

this.tr: I'm not buying — just looking.

that.tr: Just looking at it is fun.

items.explain: Look at what follows: the sentence ends with 「だけです」, or explains “I didn't do anything else” → just; 「だけで」 followed by a result (楽しい、疲れる、分かる) → this alone is enough to bring about that result.

groups.note: All mean “only, just”

items.diff: だけ works with both affirmative and negative and sounds objective; しか must be followed by a negative and carries a sense of “too few”.

this.tr: Only three people came to the party.

that.tr: Only three people came to the party (disappointingly few).

wrong.why: しか must be followed by a negative

items.explain: Look at the end of the sentence: affirmative (来た) → だけ; negative (来なかった) → しか, and the speaker feels it's “too few, not enough”.

items.diff: だけ means “only this, nothing else”; ばかり means “nothing but, always this”, usually with dissatisfaction.

this.tr: I had no time this morning, so I only ate bread.

that.tr: My little brother always eats nothing but meat.

items.explain: Look for a sense of repetition such as 「いつも」: simply saying the scope was narrow this one time → だけ; complaining that something is excessive or always that way → ばかり. English “only/just” can cover both, which is why they're easy to mix up.

groups.note: All express a guess

items.diff: Same meaning; だろう is the plain form, でしょう is the polite form.

this.tr: It'll probably rain tomorrow. (talking to oneself)

that.tr: Everyone, it will probably rain tomorrow.

items.explain: Look at who it's addressed to: talking to yourself, diaries, written texts, or close friends (mostly men) → だろう; guests, seniors, an audience (e.g. a weather forecast) → でしょう. Saying 「だろう」 to your boss would be very rude.

items.diff: だろう means you're fairly convinced; かもしれない only says “it's possible”, with little confidence.

this.tr: The sky is so dark — it'll surely rain.

that.tr: It might rain.

items.explain: Look at the adverb before it: 「きっと」 or 「たぶん」 → だろう; 「もしかしたら」 → かもしれない. When you're just raising a possibility without much confidence, use かもしれない.

groups.note: Both express the past

items.diff: Nouns and na-adjectives take でした in the past; i-adjectives change 「い」 to 「かった」 and add 「です」.

this.tr: Yesterday's test was easy.

that.tr: Yesterday's test was difficult.

wrong.why: i-adjectives can't take 「でした」

items.explain: Check the type of adjective: 簡単, 静か and きれい are na-adjectives → でした; 難しい and 寒い are i-adjectives → かったです. Note that きれい ends in 「い」 but is a na-adjective: きれいでした.

groups.note: Both come from 「に」 — で was originally 「にて」 (at a place ＋ and), meaning “doing … there”

items.title: 〜に (place of existence)
items.diff: で is followed by an action (勉強する、食べる); に is followed by existence (いる、ある、住む).

this.tr: I study at the library.

that.tr: I'm at the library.

wrong.why: 「勉強する」 is an action, so the place takes で

items.explain: で was originally 「にて」, meaning “there, (doing something)”, so an action must follow (勉強する、遊ぶ、働く); に just marks a point, followed simply by “be, exist, live” (いる、ある、住んでいる). English uses “at/in” for both, but the verb that follows tells them apart.

groups.note: Both come from 「で＋も」 — originally “even if it's…”

items.title: 〜でも (even if)
items.diff: The example-giving でも is followed by an invitation or suggestion; the concessive でも is followed by “still…, anyway”.

this.tr: If you're free, how about some tea or something?

that.tr: Even if it rains, the match will still go ahead.

items.explain: Look at the second half: an invitation or suggestion such as 「〜ませんか」 or 「〜ましょう」 → it just offers a casual example to soften the tone; something that happens anyway, unaffected → even if.

groups.note: 何でも ↔ 何も — they differ by just one 「で」

items.diff: question word＋でも takes an affirmative: “anything / everything…”; question word＋も takes a negative: “nothing…”.

this.tr: My kid eats anything.

that.tr: I haven't eaten anything since this morning.

items.explain: Look at the end of the sentence: affirmative (食べる) → 何でも、誰でも、どこでも; negative (食べていない) → 何も、誰も、どこにも. Just one 「で」 makes the meanings opposite, and the readings differ too (なんでも／なにも).

groups.note: All mean “but”

items.diff: でも starts the second sentence; けど attaches to the end of the first.

this.tr: This restaurant is expensive. But it's delicious.

that.tr: This restaurant is expensive, but it's delicious.

wrong.why: でも can't attach directly to the end of a clause

items.explain: Look at the position: the previous sentence already ended with a full stop and a new sentence begins → でも; the contrast word sticks directly onto the end of the previous clause → けど.

items.diff: Both start a sentence and mark a contrast; でも is spoken language, しかし is written language.

this.tr: Yesterday was really fun, wasn't it? But I'm a bit tired.

that.tr: This method is convenient. However, it also has problems.

items.explain: Look at the style of the sentence: a chatty tone with 「ね」 or 「ちょっと」 → でも; reports and papers in the 「である」 style → しかし. Using 「でも」 in an essay sounds too colloquial.

groups.note: Both come from the copula 「です」 — でしょう＝です＋「う」, which expresses conjecture

items.diff: でしょう is a guess — “probably”; です states something for certain.

this.tr: It will probably rain tomorrow.

that.tr: Tomorrow is Sunday.

items.explain: Ask whether it's an established fact: things you can't be sure of yourself, like the weather or someone else's situation → でしょう, often used with 「たぶん」 or 「きっと」; something fixed on the calendar → です.

groups.note: All express a guess

items.diff: Same meaning; でしょう is the polite form, だろう is the plain form.

this.tr: Everyone, it will probably rain tomorrow.

that.tr: It'll probably rain tomorrow. (talking to oneself)

items.explain: Look at who it's addressed to: guests, seniors, an audience (e.g. a weather forecast) → でしょう; talking to yourself, diaries, written texts, or close friends (mostly men) → だろう.

items.diff: でしょう means you think it's probably so; かもしれません only says it's possible, with less confidence.

this.tr: I'm sure Mr. Tanaka will come too.

that.tr: Mr. Tanaka might come too.

items.explain: Look at the adverb before it: 「きっと」 or 「たぶん」 → でしょう; 「もしかしたら」 → かもしれません. When you're just raising a possibility without much confidence, use かもしれません.

groups.note: Both express the existence of things — “there is / is located”

items.diff: (place)に N がある says “what is there”; N は (place)にある says “where N is”.

this.tr: There's a book on the desk.

that.tr: My book is on the desk.

items.explain: Think about which question you're answering: “What's on the desk?” — the new information is the thing → place に＋N がある; “Where's my book?” — the book is a known topic and the new information is the location → N は＋place にある. For specific things like “my book” or 「田中さん」, は is usually used.

groups.note: All come from ほしい (欲しい) — the speaker's inner feeling of “wanting”

items.diff: がほしい means wanting a thing; てほしい means wanting someone else to do something.

this.tr: I want a new bicycle.

that.tr: I want my dad to fix my bicycle.

items.explain: Look at what comes before 「ほしい」: noun＋が → wanting that thing; verb te-form → wanting someone else to do that action, with the doer marked by 「に」.

items.title: 〜ほしがる (someone else wants)
items.diff: ほしい only describes yourself; to say someone else wants something, use ほしがっている, and 「が」 becomes 「を」.

this.tr: I want a new game.

that.tr: My little brother wants a new game.

items.explain: Look at the subject: me (or asking the listener in a question) → がほしい; others like a brother or friend → をほしがっている. ほしい is your own inner feeling; other people's feelings can only be inferred from how they seem.

groups.note: Both mean “want”

items.diff: ほしい means wanting a thing (follows a noun); たい means wanting to do an action (follows a verb).

this.tr: I want a new car.

that.tr: I want to buy a new car.

wrong.why: After a verb, use たい

items.explain: Check whether what you want is a thing or an action: a car, money, time → がほしい; buy, go, eat → verb masu-stem＋たい. English “want” covers both, so it's easy to attach ほしい to a verb by mistake.

groups.note: が has two jobs, each with a near-synonym: marking the subject it's close to 「は」; introducing a contrast or lead-in it's close to 「けど」

items.diff: が puts the focus on the subject (who); は first raises a topic, with the focus on what follows (what about it).

this.tr: Who came? — Mr. Tanaka came.

that.tr: What time did Mr. Tanaka come?

wrong.why: A question word as subject must take が

items.explain: Look at where the focus is: wanting to know or answering “who / what” → that word takes が; raising Tanaka as a known topic first, with the point being the time or situation that follows → は.

items.diff: Almost the same meaning; が is more formal and polite, けど is more casual and colloquial.

this.tr: Excuse me, where is the station?

that.tr: Sorry, lend me a pen.

items.explain: Look at the listener and setting: strangers, guests, your boss, or in writing → が (usually after です／ます); chatting with friends → けど. Saying 「悪いが」 to a friend sounds stiff.

groups.note: Both come from 「〜が好き・〜が上手」 — the object is marked with 「が」; when what you like is an action, 「の」 turns it into a noun first

items.diff: If you like a thing, just say 「N が好き」; if you like an action, add 「の」 first.

this.tr: I like music.

that.tr: I like singing.

wrong.why: A verb needs 「の」 to become a noun first

items.explain: Look at what comes before 「が好き」: nouns like 音楽 or 猫 → attach directly; verbs like 歌う or 泳ぐ → add 「の」 (歌うのが好き). The same goes for 上手 and 嫌い.

groups.note: Both can mean “can / be good at”

items.diff: 上手 praises someone for doing something well; できる simply says you can do it.

this.tr: Mr. Tanaka, your English is really good.

that.tr: I can speak English.

items.explain: Look at who it's about: praising someone else → 上手; talking about yourself → できる (or modestly 「得意」). Saying 「上手です」 about yourself sounds like bragging; 「できる」 only says whether you can, without judging your level.

groups.note: Both come from できる (出来る) — originally “to come out, appear”, extended to “to be able to do”

items.diff: Nouns attach directly to 「ができる」; actions must be expressed as “verb dictionary form＋ことができる”.

this.tr: I can ski.

that.tr: I can swim.

wrong.why: A verb needs 「こと」 added first

items.explain: Look at what comes before 「できる」: nouns like スキー, テニス or 日本語 → N ができる; verbs like 泳ぐ or 読む → add 「こと」 first to make a noun (or just use the potential form 泳げる).

groups.note: Both can mean “can / be good at”

items.diff: できる only says you can do it; 上手 judges that it's done well.

this.tr: I can speak English.

that.tr: Mr. Tanaka, your English is really good.

items.explain: Look at who it's about: yourself → できる, which only says whether you can; praising someone else → 上手. Saying 「英語が上手です」 about yourself sounds like bragging.

groups.note: Both mean “about, around”

items.diff: ごろ follows a point in time (what time, what date); くらい follows a length of time or a quantity (how many hours, how many).

this.tr: I'll arrive at the station around three o'clock.

that.tr: It takes about three hours to get to the station.

wrong.why: A length of time can't take ごろ

items.explain: Look at what comes before: a point in time like “what time / what date” → ごろ; a length or amount like “how many hours / days / items” → くらい. In speech 「３時ぐらい」 can also mean a point in time, but 「３時間ごろ」 is always wrong.

groups.note: Both can mark where an action is directed

items.title: 〜に (destination・recipient)
items.diff: For going somewhere, both へ and に work; but only 「への」 can directly modify a noun, and giving something to someone uses 「に」.

this.tr: This is a present for my mother.

that.tr: I gave my mother a present.

wrong.why: に can't take 「の」 to modify a noun

items.explain: 「駅へ行く」 and 「駅に行く」 are almost the same; へ leans toward “direction”, に toward “point of arrival”. What matters is what follows: a noun directly (プレゼント、手紙) → only への works; an action toward a person, like 「あげる」 or 「会う」 → に.

groups.note: All are used to give advice

items.diff: ほうがいい says directly “this is better”, like a warning; たらどうですか makes a suggestion in the form of a question, sounding softer.

this.tr: You have a high fever — you'd better go to the hospital right away.

that.tr: If you're tired, why don't you rest a little?

items.explain: Consider how serious the matter is: if not doing it could cause trouble (a high fever, being late) → ほうがいい; just gently offering an idea and letting the other person decide → たらどうですか.

items.diff: ほうがいい recommends “this is better” after comparing; ばいい tells the other person a way to do it — “just do this and you'll be fine”.

this.tr: It looks like rain, so you'd better take an umbrella.

that.tr: How do I get to the station? — Just take that bus.

items.explain: Check whether it answers “what should I do?”: the other person asks how (どうすればいいですか) → ばいい, meaning “doing this is enough”; you bring it up yourself because you think it's the better option → ほうがいい.

items.diff: ほうがいい is advice with the other person's interest in mind; べきだ says “this is how it should be” on grounds of principle or duty, and sounds firmer.

this.tr: If you have a cold, you'd better go to bed early.

that.tr: You should keep your promises.

items.explain: Check whether it's about the other person's particular situation or a general principle: “this is good for you”, aimed at the person in front of you → ほうがいい; a principle or rule everyone should follow → べきだ. English “should” can cover both, but using べきだ about someone's private affairs sounds preachy.

groups.note: All express the negative “not…” — the difference is what they attach to

items.diff: i-adjectives change 「い」 to 「くない」; na-adjectives and nouns take 「じゃない」.

this.tr: This room isn't spacious.

that.tr: This room isn't clean.

wrong.why: きれい is a na-adjective, so it's きれいじゃない

items.explain: First decide the type of adjective: i-adjectives like 広い or 高い → drop い and add くない; na-adjectives like きれい, 静か or 有名 (and nouns) → じゃない. きれい and 有名 end in an 「い」 sound but are both na-adjectives.

items.diff: Verbs change to the nai-form by rule; i-adjectives first change 「い」 to 「く」 and then add 「ない」.

this.tr: It's not cold today.

that.tr: It's not raining today.

wrong.why: i-adjectives must change to 「くない」

items.explain: Look at what comes before 「ない」: verbs change by their conjugation rules (降る→降らない、食べる→食べない); i-adjectives replace the final 「い」 with 「く」 and then add ない (寒い→寒くない) — you can't just add ない directly.

groups.note: Both express the past

items.diff: The past of i-adjectives is 「かったです」; the past of nouns and na-adjectives is 「でした」.

this.tr: It was cold yesterday.

that.tr: I was free yesterday.

wrong.why: i-adjectives can't take 「でした」

items.explain: Look at how the adjective ends: i-adjectives like 寒い or 楽しい → change い to 「かった」, adding です for politeness; na-adjectives like 暇, きれい or 静か, and nouns → でした.

groups.note: Both come from 「では＋ない」 (じゃ＝では) — “is not…”

items.diff: じゃない ends the sentence and simply says “it's not A”; じゃなくて negates A and then goes on to give the correct B.

this.tr: This isn't salt.

that.tr: This isn't salt — it's sugar.

items.explain: Check whether the sentence continues after the negation: it ends there → じゃない; the correct answer follows right after (砂糖です) → じゃなくて, used to correct.

groups.note: Both mean “not…”

items.diff: Nouns and na-adjectives take 「じゃない」; i-adjectives change 「い」 to 「くない」.

this.tr: This restaurant isn't famous.

that.tr: This restaurant isn't expensive.

wrong.why: The negative of an i-adjective is 「高くない（です）」

items.explain: First check the type of adjective: na-adjectives like 有名, 静か or きれい, and nouns → じゃない; i-adjectives like 高い or 安い → くない. 有名 and きれい end in an 「い」 sound but are na-adjectives.

groups.note: Both come from 「では＋ない」 (じゃ＝では) — “is not…”

items.diff: じゃなくて negates A and then gives the correct B; じゃない ends the sentence and simply says “it's not A”.

this.tr: This isn't salt — it's sugar.

that.tr: That's not salt, you know.

items.explain: Check whether the sentence continues after the negation: the correct answer follows right after (砂糖です) → じゃなくて; it ends there → じゃない.

groups.note: ではなく ↔ だけでなく — the second just adds 「だけ」

items.diff: AではなくB means only B holds; AだけでなくB means both A and B hold.

this.tr: He speaks not English but French.

that.tr: He speaks not only English but also French.

items.explain: Look at the particle after B: 「を」 or 「です」 → ではなく, A is ruled out; 「も」 → だけでなく, A holds too, with B added. Just adding 「だけ」 changes the meaning completely.

groups.note: Both mean “during…”

items.diff: 〜中 only follows nouns; if a verb (〜ている) comes before, use 「間」.

this.tr: Please turn off your phone during the meeting.

that.tr: It rained while I was asleep.

wrong.why: 中 can't follow a verb — use 間

items.explain: Check whether a noun or a verb comes before: nouns like 会議, 授業 or 夏休み → 〜中 (会議中、夏休み中); verbs like 寝ている or 日本にいる → 〜間／〜間に. A noun can also take 「会議の間」, but needs 「の」.

groups.note: All are the same 「か」 — its core meaning is “uncertainty”

items.diff: 何を〜か asks what exactly; 何か〜か asks “do you want … something?”, answered with はい／いいえ.

this.tr: What will you eat? — I'll have sushi.

that.tr: Will you eat something? — Yes, I will.

items.explain: Look at what follows the question word: a particle like 「を」 or 「が」 → it really asks “what”, and the answer gives specifics; 「か」 directly → 「何か」 means “something”, and the whole sentence only asks yes or no, so the answer is 「はい／いいえ」.

items.diff: A question with a question word just adds 「か」; without a question word, asking “whether or not” takes 「かどうか」.

this.tr: I don't know when he's coming.

that.tr: I don't know whether he's coming tomorrow.

wrong.why: With a question word, don't add 「どうか」

items.explain: Check whether the embedded question has a question word: いつ, どこ, 誰 → just add か; no question word, only asking “coming or not, right or not” → かどうか.

groups.note: そうですか ↔ そうですね — they differ only in the last kana

items.diff: そうですか responds to news — “oh, I see”; そうですね agrees with the other person — “yes, that's right”.

this.tr: Tomorrow is a day off, you know. — Oh, is it? (I see.)

that.tr: It's hot today, isn't it? — Yes, it is.

items.explain: Look at what the other person said: news you didn't know before (〜よ) → そうですか (falling intonation); something you both feel, where they're seeking agreement (〜ね) → そうですね. Answering “It's hot today, isn't it?” with 「そうですか」 sounds as if you doubt them.

groups.note: たから ↔ てから — they differ by just one kana

items.diff: たから means “because … happened”; てから means “after doing …”.

this.tr: I've eaten, so I'm full.

that.tr: I'll go out after I eat.

items.explain: The only difference is た vs て: ta-form＋から gives a reason, and the second half is the resulting outcome (おなかがいっぱい); te-form＋から gives time order, and the second half is what you do next (出かける).

groups.note: Both express a reason

items.diff: から is subjective and colloquial, and can also end a sentence as 「〜からです」; ので is objective and polite, and can only be used mid-sentence.

this.tr: The reason I was late is that the train stopped.

that.tr: The train stopped, so I was late.

wrong.why: ので can't end a sentence with 「です」

items.explain: Look at the position and setting: at the end of a sentence answering “why” → only から works (〜からです); mid-sentence when explaining a reason to a teacher or boss → ので sounds more objective, less like an excuse; speaking casually to friends, or followed by a command or invitation → から is more natural.

groups.note: まで ↔ までに — they differ by just one 「に」

items.diff: から〜まで says you keep doing something over a period; までに gives a deadline — just finish before then.

this.tr: I work from nine to five.

that.tr: I'll be back by five.

wrong.why: Handing in homework is a one-time action, so use までに

items.explain: Look at the verb that follows: continuous actions like 働く, 待つ or 寝る → まで; one-time actions like 帰る, 出す or 終わる → までに, meaning “by then at the latest”.

groups.note: Both express a range “from… to…”

items.diff: から〜まで has clear start and end points; から〜にかけて only gives a rough range, often in weather reports and news.

this.tr: Class is from nine to twelve.

that.tr: It will probably rain from tonight into tomorrow.

items.explain: Check whether it's a precise time: things with clear start and end times, like classes or business hours → から〜まで; a vague period or area like “tonight into tomorrow” in a weather forecast → から〜にかけて.

groups.note: 〜方（かた）↔ 〜方（ほう）がいい — the same kanji, but different readings and meanings

items.diff: masu-stem＋方 is read 「かた」 and means “the way of doing…”; ta-form＋方がいい is read 「ほう」 and means “you'd better…”.

this.tr: Please teach me how to write this kanji.

that.tr: You'd better write kanji by hand.

items.explain: Look at what comes before 「方」: verb masu-stem (書き、読み)＋方 → read 「かた」, a noun meaning “way of writing”, preceded by 「の」; verb ta-form (書いた)＋方がいい → read 「ほう」, advising “you'd better do this”.

groups.note: All express a contrast — “although…, but…”

items.title: 〜が (contrast)
items.diff: けど is more colloquial, used between friends; が is more formal, used in formal situations, writing and emails.

this.tr: This place is pricey, but it's really good!

that.tr: The prices at this restaurant are high, but the food is truly excellent.

items.explain: Look at the tone of the whole sentence: a chatty tone with 「よ」 and dropped particles → けど; formal wording like 「です・ます」 with 「大変」, in reports, emails or speeches → が. 「高いですけど」 is also possible, but formal writing generally uses が.

items.title: 〜のに (even though…)
items.diff: けど is just an objective contrast and can be followed by an intention or invitation; のに carries surprise and dissatisfaction, and can't be followed by an intention or invitation.

this.tr: It's a bit expensive, but I'll buy it.

that.tr: Even though it was so expensive, it broke right away.

wrong.why: のに can't be followed by an intention or invitation like 「〜よう」

items.explain: Look at the second half: the speaker's own plan, invitation or request (買おう、〜てください) → only けど works; a result contrary to expectations, with dissatisfaction or regret (すぐ壊れた) → only のに conveys that “even though…” feeling.

items.title: でも (sentence-initial: but)
items.diff: けど attaches to the end of the first clause, joining two into one sentence; でも starts the second sentence, so the first must be finished.

this.tr: These clothes are expensive, but they're cute.

that.tr: These clothes are expensive. But they're cute.

wrong.why: でも can't attach to the end of a clause — end the sentence with 「。」 first

items.explain: Look at the position: 「けど」 sticks right onto the end of the previous clause (高いけど、); 「でも」 must come after a complete sentence closed with 「。」, at the start of the next one. Since English “but” can go either way, learners easily write ✗高いでも.

groups.note: All are built from the prefixes 「こ・そ・あ・ど」 — the prefix shows distance, the ending shows the category

items.diff: この must be followed by a noun; これ stands alone and can itself be the subject or object.

this.tr: This book is mine.

that.tr: This is my book.

wrong.why: この must be followed by a noun

items.explain: Look at what comes right after: a noun (本、人、店) → この; a particle 「は・が・を」 → これ. Tip: words ending in 「〜の」 act like adjectives such as “this…” — a noun must always follow.

items.diff: この＋noun points to this particular one in front of you; ここ refers to this place, and to modify a noun it becomes 「ここの」.

this.tr: This ramen is delicious, isn't it?

that.tr: The ramen here is delicious, you know.

items.explain: Check whether it's about a “thing” or a “place”: eating the noodles and saying “this bowl” → この; recommending to a friend “the ramen at this shop (this place)” → ここの. 「ここ」 is itself a place noun, so like any noun it needs 「の」 to modify another noun.

items.diff: この points to a specific one; こんな means “like this, this kind of”, describing type and nature.

this.tr: Excuse me, I'll take this bag.

that.tr: I'd love to have a bag like this someday.

items.explain: You want exactly the one in front of you → この; you see someone's bag and want “one like it” → こんな. It's the difference between “this” and “this kind of / like this”.

groups.note: All are built from the prefixes 「こ・そ・あ・ど」 — the prefix shows distance, the ending shows the category

items.diff: ここ refers to a place, asked about with 「どこ」; これ refers to a thing, asked about with 「何」.

this.tr: Where is this (place)?

that.tr: What is this?

items.explain: Check whether it's a place or a thing: asking “what place is this?” → ここ＋どこ; asking “what thing is this?” → これ＋何. Something you're holding or pointing at can't be ここ.

items.diff: ここの＋noun means “of this place”; この＋noun points to this particular one in front of you.

this.tr: The ramen here is delicious, you know.

that.tr: This ramen is delicious, isn't it?

items.explain: Recommending to a friend “the ramen at this shop (this place)” → ここの; eating the noodles and saying “this bowl” → この. 「ここ」 is a place noun and needs 「の」 to modify another noun; 「この」 already contains 「の」 and attaches directly to a noun.

groups.note: どこ ↔ どこか — they differ by just one 「か」

items.diff: どこ asks “where”, and the answer is a place; どこか means “somewhere”, so you answer “yes / no” first.

this.tr: Where are you going on Sunday?

that.tr: Are you going anywhere on Sunday?

items.explain: Just one 「か」 makes the answers completely different: どこへ → “To Kyoto”; どこかへ → “Yes, to Kyoto” or “No, nowhere”. When you hear 「どこか」, answer 「はい／いいえ」 first.

groups.note: All are built from the prefixes 「こ・そ・あ・ど」 — the prefix shows distance, the ending shows the category

items.diff: これ stands alone, directly followed by 「は・が・を」; この must be followed by a noun.

this.tr: This is my book.

that.tr: This book is mine.

wrong.why: To modify a noun, use 「この」

items.explain: Look at what comes right after: a particle 「は・が・を」 → これ; a noun (本、人、店) → この. 「これ」 is a pronoun and can't sit directly in front of a noun.

items.diff: これ refers to a thing, asked about with 「何」; ここ refers to a place, asked about with 「どこ」.

this.tr: What is this?

that.tr: Where is this (place)?

items.explain: Check whether it's a thing or a place: the ending 「れ」 refers to things and pairs with 「何」; the ending 「こ」 refers to places and pairs with 「どこ」.

groups.note: Both are 「〜ができる」 (出来る: can do, be able) — ことができる＝こと (turns an action into a noun)＋ができる

items.title: 〜ができる
items.diff: Nouns attach directly to 「ができる」; actions must be expressed as “verb＋ことができる”.

this.tr: I can write letters in Japanese.

that.tr: I can speak Japanese.

wrong.why: A verb needs 「こと」 added

items.explain: Look at what comes before 「ができる」: nouns (日本語、テニス、料理) → attach directly; verbs (書く、泳ぐ) → must add 「こと」 first to become a noun. English just says “can…” for both, so it's easy to leave out こと.

groups.note: Both mean “can, be able to”

items.title: 〜られる (potential)
items.diff: ことができる is formal and written, often used in rules and explanations; the potential form is short and more common in everyday conversation.

this.tr: At this library you may borrow up to five books.

that.tr: You can borrow up to five books at this library, you know.

items.explain: Same meaning — look at the setting and the particle: notices, explanations, formal occasions → ことができます, with the object keeping 「を」 (本を借りる); chatting with friends → the potential form is more natural, and the object often becomes 「が」 (本が借りられる).

groups.note: Both can turn an action into a noun — “the act of doing…”

items.diff: こと is more abstract and can be used in 「趣味は〜ことです」; の is more concrete and colloquial, often used in 「〜のが好き」.

this.tr: My hobby is taking photos.

that.tr: I like taking photos.

wrong.why: When 「AはBです」 explains a hobby or dream, only こと works

items.explain: Look at the sentence structure: 「趣味は／夢は〜」 ending with 「です」 → only ことです; before 「好き・上手・嫌い」 both work, but 「のが好き」 is more natural in conversation.

groups.note: All express “change”

items.title: 〜くする・〜にする (make it change)
items.diff: くなる／になる means it changes naturally; くする／にする means someone deliberately makes it change.

this.tr: The sun came in and the room got warm.

that.tr: I turned on the air conditioner and warmed up the room.

items.explain: Look at the particle and the cause: 「部屋が」＋a natural cause (日が当たる) → くなる; 「部屋を」＋a person's action (エアコンをつける) → くする. なる takes が, する takes を.

items.diff: Adjectives and nouns use くなる／になる; verbs use ようになる.

this.tr: I got better at swimming.

that.tr: I became able to swim.

wrong.why: A verb can't attach directly to になる

items.explain: Look at the word before 「なる」: 上手 is a na-adjective → になる (寒い → 寒くなる, 医者 → 医者になる); 泳げる is a verb → add 「よう」 first to make ようになる. English uses “become / get…” for everything, so the most common mistake is ✗泳げるになった.

groups.note: All express “about” or a “degree”

items.diff: くらい follows a length of time (how many hours); ごろ follows a point in time (what time).

this.tr: I slept about seven hours yesterday.

that.tr: I went to bed around eleven yesterday.

wrong.why: ごろ only follows a point in time; for duration, use くらい

items.explain: Look at the word before: 「〜時間」, 「〜日」 or 「〜年」 is a span of time → くらい／ぐらい; a point in time like 「〜時」 or 「〜月」 → ごろ. In speech some people say 「11時ぐらい」, but 「〜時間ごろ」 is always wrong.

items.title: 〜ほど (degree)
items.diff: When expressing degree, the two are mostly interchangeable; when meaning “at least this much”, only くらい works.

this.tr: However busy you are, you can at least make a phone call, right?

that.tr: My feet hurt so much I can't walk anymore.

wrong.why: To mean “at least, at a minimum”, only くらい works

items.explain: Check whether the example is “extreme” or “easy”: using something extreme to show degree (歩けないほど／くらい) → both work; naming the bare minimum, the easiest thing, as a demand (電話ぐらい) → only くらい, often with a reproachful tone.

groups.note: まだ〜ていない ↔ まだ〜ている — they differ only by 「ない」

items.title: まだ〜ている (still…)
items.diff: まだ〜ていない means “not … yet”; まだ〜ている means “still …ing”.

this.tr: It's already midnight, but my little brother hasn't gone to bed yet.

that.tr: It's already noon, but my little brother is still asleep.

items.explain: It's the same 「まだ」 — check whether the sentence ends with 「ない」: まだ寝ていない → going to sleep, which should have happened, hasn't happened yet; まだ寝ている → the state of sleeping still hasn't ended. Just as “not asleep yet” and “still asleep” differ by a word or two, the Japanese differs only by 「ない」.

groups.note: All mean “not … yet” up to now

items.diff: まだ〜ていない just objectively says “not yet”; なかなか〜ない means “just won't…”, with impatience from waiting.

this.tr: The bus hasn't come yet.

that.tr: I've been waiting for thirty minutes, and the bus just won't come.

items.explain: Look for a feeling of impatient waiting: just reporting the current situation → まだ来ていない; you've waited a long time and keep being disappointed (30分も待っているのに) → なかなか来ない. Also, なかなか is followed by a plain 「ない」, not 「ていない」.

items.title: 〜たことがない (have never…)
items.diff: まだ〜ていない means something you plan to do is “not done yet”; 〜たことがない means you've “never done it” in your life.

this.tr: I haven't seen that movie yet. I'm going to see it next week.

that.tr: I've never seen a horror movie, not even once.

items.explain: English can say “I haven't seen it” for both. Look at the surrounding words: you plan to do it later (来週見に行く) → まだ〜ていない; it's about your life experience so far, regardless of plans (一度も) → 〜たことがない.

groups.note: Both come from 「まで」 — drawing a finish line for an action

items.diff: まで means continuing until then; までに means doing it once before then.

this.tr: I'll wait until five.

that.tr: I'll be back by five.

wrong.why: 「出す」 is a one-time action, so use までに

items.explain: Look at the verb that follows: actions that can continue, like 待つ, 働く or 勉強する → まで; actions completed in a moment, like 帰る, 出す or 着く → までに.

groups.note: Both can mean “even…”

items.title: 〜さえ (even…)
items.diff: まで means “even this is added on”, mostly for adding to or expanding something; さえ means “even the most basic thing”, mostly used with a negative.

this.tr: Not only is it raining — even the wind has picked up.

that.tr: My fever is so high I can't even drink water.

items.explain: See which way the sentence goes: one more item added after 「〜だけでなく」, with things getting worse (or better) → まで; naming the most basic, easiest thing that even that can't be done → さえ, usually followed by a negative.

groups.note: Both come from 前 (まえ) — originally “in front” in space

items.title: 〜の前 (position)
items.diff: activity＋の前に means “before” in time; place＋の前に means “in front of” in space.

this.tr: I wash my hands before eating.

that.tr: There's a bank in front of the station.

items.explain: Both sentences use 「〜の前に」 — look at the noun before it: activities like 食事, 会議 or 試験 → “before” in time; places or objects like 駅, 家 or 机 → “in front of” in space, often followed by 「あります・います」.

groups.note: All mean “(do) before…”

items.diff: 前に says which of two things comes first; までに gives a deadline — just finish before then.

this.tr: Please close the window before you go out.

that.tr: Please submit your report by Friday.

items.explain: Look at what comes before: another action (出かける、寝る) → 前に, only giving the order; a date or time (金曜日、３時) as a deadline → までに, stressing “by then at the latest” — any time before that is fine.

items.title: 〜うちに (while still…)
items.diff: 前に follows an action; うちに mostly follows a state, with the sense of “hurry and do it while it's still…”.

this.tr: I want to travel the world before I get old.

that.tr: I want to travel the world while I'm young.

wrong.why: 前に can't follow an adjective

items.explain: Check whether an action or a state comes before: actions of change like 年を取る or 暗くなる → 前に; states that will fade, like 若い, 元気な or 明るい → うちに, stressing “while you still can”.

groups.note: All can be used to invite or suggest

items.diff: ませんか first asks about the other person's wishes; ましょう pushes to do something together, assuming they'll agree.

this.tr: If you'd like, would you like to see a movie together?

that.tr: Sure, sounds good. Let's watch it together.

items.explain: Look at the order in the conversation: a first invitation, not knowing if the other person wants to → ませんか (often with 「よかったら」); they've already agreed, or everyone has already decided → ましょう. Opening with ましょう can sound like you're deciding for them.

items.diff: ませんか asks the other person to do something (together); ましょうか can mean “let me do it for you”.

this.tr: Shall we walk to the station together?

that.tag: Let me do it for you
that.tr: That looks heavy. Shall I carry your bag?

items.explain: Look at who does the action: the other person, or the two of you together → ませんか; I offer to do it for them → ましょうか.

items.title: 〜ない？ (invitation)
items.diff: ませんか is polite, used with superiors or people you don't know well; 〜ない？ is casual, used between friends and family.

this.tr: Professor, would you like to have lunch together?

that.tr: Hey, wanna grab lunch together?

items.explain: Look at who it's addressed to: seniors and superiors like 「先生」 or 「部長」 → ませんか; friends and family (ねえ、〜くん) → 「〜ない？」 with rising intonation. Both use a negative question to invite.

items.title: 〜はいかがですか (offering)
items.diff: ませんか follows an action, inviting the other person to do it; 〜はいかがですか follows a thing, offering it to them.

this.tr: Would you like to have some tea or something?

that.tr: How about some tea?

items.explain: Look at what comes before: a verb (飲み、行き)＋ませんか, often with 「でも」, invites the other person to do an action; a noun (お茶、コーヒー)＋はいかがですか puts the thing right in front of them, typically said by a host or shop staff to a guest.

groups.note: All come from 「う」, which expresses intention — ましょう＝ます＋う

items.diff: ましょう means “let's … together”; adding 「か」 to make ましょうか turns it into “shall I…?” or consulting the other person.

this.tr: Come on, let's all clean up together.

that.tr: Shall I do the cleaning?

items.explain: Look at the subject and 「か」: everyone doing it together, with the speaker taking the lead → ましょう; me doing it alone for the other person, or asking their opinion → ましょうか. When offering help, 「手伝いましょう」 sounds pushy — say 「手伝いましょうか」.

items.diff: ましょう is polite; the volitional form 「〜(よ)う」 is its casual form, used between friends.

this.tr: Sir, shall we get going soon?

that.tr: Hey, let's get going soon.

items.explain: Look at who it's addressed to: superiors, seniors, people you don't know well → 行きましょう; friends, family → 行こう, 食べよう. Both mean the same — stating your own intention while drawing the other person in.

groups.note: Both can invite the other person to do something together

items.diff: ましょう pushes to act together, assuming the other person agrees; ませんか first asks whether they want to.

this.tr: Sure, sounds good. Let's watch it together.

that.tr: If you'd like, would you like to see a movie together?

items.explain: Look at the order in the conversation: they've already agreed, or everyone has already decided → ましょう; a first invitation, not knowing if they want to → ませんか (often with 「よかったら」). Usually you ask 「〜ませんか」 first, and say 「〜ましょう」 once they agree.

groups.note: All come from 「う」, which expresses intention — ましょう＝ます＋う

items.diff: ましょうか means “shall I…?” or consulting the other person; without 「か」, ましょう directly pushes “let's … together”.

this.tr: Shall I do the cleaning?

that.tr: Come on, let's all clean up together.

items.explain: Look at the subject and 「か」: me doing it alone for the other person, or asking their opinion → ましょうか; everyone doing it together, with the speaker taking the lead → ましょう.

items.title: 〜(よ)うか (casual)
items.diff: ましょうか is polite; 「〜(よ)うか」 is its casual form, used with family and friends.

this.tr: Professor, shall I carry that bag for you?

that.tr: Mom, shall I carry that bag?

items.explain: Same meaning — look at who it's addressed to: teachers, bosses, guests → 持ちましょうか; family, friends → 持とうか (for godan verbs, the 「う」-row sound changes to the 「お」-row ＋う).

groups.note: Both can be used to suggest or invite

items.diff: ましょうか can mean “let me do it for you”; ませんか asks the other person to do something (together).

this.tag: Let me do it for you
this.tr: That looks heavy. Shall I carry your bag?

that.tr: Shall we walk to the station together?

items.explain: Look at who does the action: I offer to do it for them → ましょうか; the other person, or the two of you together → ませんか.

groups.note: Both come from the polite auxiliary 「ます」 — ませんか＝ません＋the question marker 「か」

items.diff: ません is a negative, “don't…”; adding 「か」 to make ませんか usually turns it into an invitation, “would you like to…?”.

this.tr: I'm not going to the movies tomorrow.

that.tr: Would you like to go to the movies tomorrow?

items.explain: Just one 「か」 makes the difference: a sentence ending in 「ません。」 → you say you won't do it; ending in 「ませんか」 → usually an invitation, answered with 「いいですね」 or 「ええ、ぜひ」 — not 「はい、行きません」.

groups.note: Both express the negative, differing only in politeness

items.diff: ません is the polite negative; ない is the plain negative, with the same meaning.

this.tr: Professor, I won't drink today.

that.tr: Sorry, I'm not drinking today.

items.explain: Look at who it's addressed to: teachers, bosses, strangers → 飲みません; friends, family → 飲まない. Note the conjugation: ません attaches to the masu-stem (飲み), ない to the nai-form stem (飲ま).

groups.note: Both come from the particle 「も」 — “also”: 「何も〜ない」 is literally “not … even anything”

items.diff: noun＋も means “… too”; question word＋も＋negative means “nothing at all, no one at all”.

this.tr: I don't drink coffee. I don't drink juice either.

that.tr: I haven't drunk anything since this morning.

items.explain: Look at what comes before 「も」: a specific thing (ジュース) → “too / either”, usually after an item of the same kind was mentioned (コーヒーは…); a question word (何、誰、どこ)＋も followed by a negative → “nothing / no one”, a total negation, not “too”.

groups.note: All come from the formal noun 「の」 — presenting something as “the situation”

items.diff: んです explains a situation and the sentence ends there; んですが first explains the situation, then goes on to a request or question.

this.tr: Sorry I'm late. The train stopped.

that.tr: Excuse me, I'm lost — where is the station?

items.explain: Check whether anything follows: the sentence ends with 「んです。」, explaining a reason → んです; 「んですが、」 followed by a request or question (駅はどこですか、〜てもいいですか) → it's a lead-in.

items.diff: んですか politely asks about the situation; 〜の？ is its casual form, used with friends and family.

this.tr: Professor, what's the matter?

that.tr: Hey, what's wrong?

items.explain: Both ask the reason after noticing how someone looks — look at who it's addressed to: teachers, bosses, people you don't know well → 〜んですか; friends, family → 「〜の？」 with rising intonation.

groups.note: Both come from the classical 「なり」 — 「な」 to modify nouns, 「に」 to modify verbs

items.title: 〜に (na-adjective modifying a verb)
items.diff: A na-adjective modifying a noun takes 「な」; modifying a verb, it takes 「に」.

this.tr: I study in a quiet room.

that.tr: Please speak quietly in the library.

wrong.why: To modify a verb, use 「に」

items.explain: Look at the word right after: a noun (部屋、人、町) → 静かな; a verb (話す、歩く、書く) → 静かに. English marks this with “quiet / quietly”; Japanese does it with な and に.

groups.note: All go before a noun to modify it

items.title: 名詞＋の＋名詞
items.diff: na-adjective＋な＋noun; noun＋の＋noun.

this.tr: I received some beautiful flowers.

that.tr: I received some roses.

wrong.why: A na-adjective modifying a noun needs 「な」

items.explain: First decide what kind of word comes before: a describing word that can take 「とても〜」 (きれい、静か、有名) → な; the name of a person, place or thing (バラ、日本、私) → の. In English both simply go in front of the noun, so the classic mistake is ✗きれいの花.

items.title: い形容詞＋名詞
items.diff: na-adjectives need 「な」; i-adjectives attach directly to the noun with nothing added.

this.tr: I went to a famous restaurant.

that.tr: I went to a restaurant with great food.

wrong.why: i-adjectives attach directly to nouns, without な

items.explain: Look at how the adjective ends: i-adjectives ending in 「い」 (おいしい、高い) attach directly to nouns; na-adjectives (有名、静か) need 「な」. Note that きれい ends in 「い」 but is a na-adjective: きれいな花.

groups.note: Both come from the sentence-final exclamatory 「な」 — かな＝the question 「か」＋the exclamatory 「な」

items.diff: なあ expresses an exclamation or a wish; かな adds a questioning 「か」, wondering to yourself “I wonder if…?”.

this.tr: I hope it's sunny tomorrow.

that.tr: I wonder if it'll be sunny tomorrow.

items.explain: Check whether 「か」 comes before 「な」: no → a simple exclamation or wish; with 「か」 → you're unsure and asking yourself.

groups.note: Prohibitive 「な」 ↔ negative 「ない」 — both contain 「な」

items.diff: dictionary form＋な is a prohibition, “don't…!”; nai-form＋ない is a negative, “not…”.

this.tr: Don't touch that!

that.tr: I won't touch that.

items.explain: Look at the verb form before 「な」: dictionary form (触る)＋な → ordering the other person “don't do it”, with the verb itself in the affirmative; nai-form stem (触ら)＋ない → stating “I don't do it”. Don't mistake 「〜るな」 or 「〜くな」 for a plain negative.

groups.note: The exclamatory 「なあ」 is close to 「ね」; the prohibitive 「な」 is close to 「ないでください」

items.diff: なあ is mostly an exclamation to yourself; ね is said to the listener, seeking agreement.

this.tr: Ah, it's so hot.

that.tr: It's really hot today, isn't it?

items.explain: Check whether there's a listener: talking to yourself, needing no reply → なあ, usually after the plain form; making small talk and hoping for a “yes, it is” → ね, which can follow 「です」.

items.diff: dictionary form＋な is a rude, forceful prohibition; ないでください is a polite request.

this.tr: No smoking here!

that.tr: Excuse me, please don't smoke here.

items.explain: Look at who it's addressed to and the setting: guests, strangers, superiors → ないでください; angry scolding, urgent shouts or signs → 〜な. Saying 「〜な」 to someone's face is very rude.

groups.note: Both can express “at the same time”

items.diff: ながら means one person doing two things at once; 間 sets a stretch of time as the background, and the two parts can have different people.

this.tr: I listened to music while I cooked.

that.tr: While my mom was cooking, I was listening to music.

wrong.why: With ながら, both actions must be done by the same person

items.explain: Look at the subjects of the two actions: the same person → ながら; different people (母が…, 私は…) → 間.

items.title: 〜て (accompanying state)
items.diff: ながら means two actions happening at the same time; て means doing something while keeping the resulting state of the first action.

this.tr: I read the newspaper while listening to music.

that.tr: I read the newspaper with my glasses on.

items.explain: Look at the first verb: ongoing actions like 聞く, 歌う, 歩く → ながら; actions that leave a state once done, like かける, 座る, 持つ → て. English “with glasses on” or “sitting down and…” both need the te-form.

groups.note: Negative 「ない」 ↔ prohibitive 「な」 — both contain 「な」

items.title: 〜な (prohibition)
items.diff: nai-form + ない is a negative, “don't / won't…”; dictionary form + な is a prohibition, “Don't…!”.

this.tr: I won't touch that.

that.tr: Don't touch that!

items.explain: Look at the verb form before 「な」: nai-form (触ら) + ない → a statement, “I don't do it”; dictionary form (触る) + な → an order to someone, “Don't do it” — the verb itself is affirmative.

groups.note: All express negation — look at what comes before and who you're talking to

items.title: 〜ません
items.diff: ない is the plain negative; ません is the polite negative — same meaning.

this.tr: Sorry, I'm not drinking today.

that.tr: Sensei, I won't be drinking today.

items.explain: Look at who you're talking to: friends, family → 飲まない; teachers, bosses, strangers → 飲みません. Note the forms: ない attaches to the nai-form (飲ま), ません to the masu-stem (飲み).

items.diff: A verb's negative is nai-form + ない; an i-adjective's negative changes 「い」 to 「くない」.

this.tr: I don't eat this dish.

that.tr: This dish isn't tasty.

wrong.why: For an i-adjective, drop 「い」 and add 「くない」

items.explain: Look at what kind of word comes before: a verb (食べる) → 食べない; an i-adjective (おいしい) → drop 「い」 and add 「くない」. The negative of 「いい」 is 「よくない」.

items.diff: Verbs are negated with 「ない」; nouns and na-adjectives are negated with 「じゃない」.

this.tr: Tanaka doesn't come to school.

that.tr: Tanaka isn't a student.

wrong.why: A noun is negated with 「じゃない」

items.explain: Look at what comes before: a verb (来る) → 来ない; a noun (学生) or na-adjective (元気) → じゃない (polite: ではありません). The difference between “doesn't (do)” and “isn't (a…)” in English is the difference between ない and じゃない in Japanese.

groups.note: Both come from 「いけない」 (行けない = “won't do / no good”) — not doing it is no good = must; doing it is no good = forbidden

items.diff: ないといけない is “not doing it is no good” = must; てはいけない is “doing it is no good” = must not.

this.tr: I have to take my medicine every day.

that.tr: You must not drink alcohol while taking medicine.

items.explain: Look at what comes before 「いけない」: 「ないと」 (if you don't) → must do; 「ては／では」 (if you do) → not allowed. Only the negative in front differs, yet the meanings are exact opposites.

groups.note: Both mean “must”

items.diff: ないといけない is conversational, mostly about your own specific situation; なければならない is more formal, mostly for rules and in writing.

this.tr: It's already ten. I have to go home.

that.tr: In Japan, cars must drive on the left.

items.explain: Look at what is being talked about: your own immediate situation (もう10時だ) → ないといけない sounds more natural; objective obligations in laws, rules or writing → なければならない. They mean the same, and swapping them isn't wrong.

groups.note: Both come from the negative 「ないで」 — “without doing…”

items.diff: ないで + ください asks someone not to do something; ないで + another verb means “did… without…”.

this.tr: Please don't forget your umbrella.

that.tr: I went out without an umbrella.

items.explain: Look at what follows 「ないで」: 「ください」 → asking someone not to do it; another verb (出かけた, 寝た) → describing doing B without having done A.

groups.note: Both mean “don't… / not allowed to…”

items.diff: ないでください is a request and sounds polite; てはいけません states a rule, and sounds condescending if said to guests or superiors.

this.tr: Excuse me, please don't take photos here.

that.tr: Taking photos inside the art museum is not allowed.

items.explain: Look at the speaker's position: asking someone face to face to cooperate, especially guests or strangers → ないでください; explaining a rule, or a teacher to students, a parent to a child → てはいけません.

items.title: 〜な (prohibition)
items.diff: ないでください is a polite request; dictionary form + な is a rude, forceful prohibition.

this.tr: Excuse me, please don't smoke here.

that.tr: No smoking here!

items.explain: Look at who you're talking to and the situation: guests, strangers, superiors → ないでください; scolding in anger, shouting in an emergency, or on signs → 〜な. Note that 〜な follows the dictionary form (吸う), not the nai-form.

groups.note: Both come from the negative 「ないで」 — “without doing…”

items.diff: ないで + another verb means “did… without…”; ないで + ください asks someone not to do something.

this.tr: I went out without an umbrella.

that.tr: Please don't forget your umbrella.

items.explain: Look at what follows 「ないで」: another verb (出かけた, 寝た) → describing doing B without having done A; 「ください」 → asking someone not to do it.

groups.note: ないで ↔ なくて — both are 「ない」 + te-form, differing by just a kana or two

items.diff: ないで means “without… (did something else)”; なくて gives a reason, “because… didn't…”.

this.tr: I didn't take the bus; I walked.

that.tr: The bus just wouldn't come, and I was stuck.

items.explain: Look at the second half: another action you then did yourself (歩いて行った) → ないで; a result or feeling caused by the “didn't…” (困った, 遅れた) → なくて.

groups.note: Both mean “not doing A (and doing B)”

items.diff: Same meaning: ないで is for everyday speech; ずに is more literary, and 「する」 becomes 「せずに」.

this.tr: I took the exam without studying.

that.tr: I took the exam without studying.

wrong.why: 「する」 must become 「せずに」

items.explain: Both mean the same; look at register and how they attach: in speech, ないで (しないで) is more common; in writing or formal situations, ずに is common. ずに replaces 「ない」 in the nai-form (言わ + ずに), but 「する」 is an exception: it's 「せずに」.

groups.note: All come from the conditional of 「ない」 (なければ／なくては) — “if you don't…, it's no good”

items.diff: なければならない is complete and formal; なきゃ／なくちゃ are spoken contractions, often with the second half dropped, used only with people you're close to.

this.tr: Students must attend class.

that.tr: Oh, it's already eight. I've gotta go.

items.explain: なきゃ = なければ, なくちゃ = なくては, and the following 「ならない／いけない」 is often dropped. Look at the situation: rules, writing, formal settings → なければならない; talking to yourself, or to friends and family → なきゃ・なくちゃ.

groups.note: All mean “must / should”

items.diff: なければならない is more formal, mostly for rules and in writing; ないといけない is conversational, mostly about your own specific situation.

this.tr: In Japan, cars must drive on the left.

that.tr: It's already ten. I have to go home.

items.explain: Look at what is being talked about: objective obligations in laws, rules or writing → なければならない; your own immediate situation (もう10時だ) → ないといけない sounds more natural. They mean the same, and swapping them isn't wrong.

items.diff: なければならない is a rule or objective obligation; べきだ is the speaker's personal opinion that something “should” be done.

this.tr: In Japan, cars must drive on the left.

that.tr: I think young people should read more books.

items.explain: Look at whether it's a rule or a view: laws, rules, things that simply must be done → なければならない; the speaker's own claim or advice, often with 「と思う」 → べきだ. English “must / have to” mostly corresponds to なければならない, and “should” to べきだ.

groups.note: Both come from 「いい」 — 「ても + いい」 = “it's fine even so”: fine to do it (てもいい) / fine not to (なくてもいい)

items.title: 〜てもいい (permission)
items.diff: てもいい is “you may do it”; なくてもいい is “you don't have to do it” — check whether what comes before 「ても」 is affirmative or negative.

this.tr: If you have a fever, you don't have to go to school tomorrow.

that.tr: Your fever has gone down, so you can go to school tomorrow.

items.explain: Look at what comes before 「ても」: 「行って」 is affirmative → permission to do it; 「行かなく」 is negative → fine not to, no need. When asked 「〜なくてもいいですか」, answering 「はい」 means you really don't have to.
