groups.note: Both mean “no need to / don't have to”

items.diff: なくてもいい objectively says “it's fine not to”; ことはない urges someone “there's no need for that”, often to reassure them.

this.tr: Tomorrow is a day off, so you don't need to come to the office.

that.tr: There's no need to worry so much.

items.explain: ことはない follows the dictionary form and often goes with 「そんなに」 or 「わざわざ」, urging someone not to do something unnecessary; なくてもいい follows the negative form, simply states there's no need, and can also be used to ask 「〜なくてもいいですか」.

items.title: 〜ずに済む
items.diff: なくてもいい says “there's no need to do it”; ずに済む says “I would have had to, but luckily I didn't need to after all”.

this.tr: The station is close, so you don't need to take a taxi.

that.tr: A friend drove me, so luckily I didn't have to take a taxi.

items.explain: Look at the tense and tone: ずに済んだ is usually past tense and says “something I would have had to do was avoided thanks to some circumstance”, with a sense of relief; なくてもいい just states there's no need now or in the future.

groups.note: Both go at the end of a sentence and add the speaker's tone

items.diff: ね is for things the listener also knows, seeking agreement; よ tells the listener something they don't know.

this.tr: (Both eating) This cake is really good, isn't it?

that.tr: This cake is really good, you know. Try some.

items.explain: Look at whether the listener knows: you're both eating and they feel the same → ね; they haven't tried it yet and you're telling them, recommending it → よ, often followed by urging like 「食べてみて」.

items.title: 〜なあ (exclamation)
items.diff: ね is said to someone, seeking agreement; なあ is mostly an exclamation to yourself.

this.tr: Mr. Tanaka, it's really hot today, isn't it?

that.tr: (Muttering alone) Ugh, it's so hot today.

items.explain: Look at whether there's a listener: calling someone by name, speaking to someone with 「です」 → ね; muttering to yourself, an inner exclamation → なあ, which is why 「なあ」 is normally used with plain form, not with 「です」.

groups.note: Both come from the case particle 「に」 — marking the goal a movement reaches

items.diff: place + に is “where you go”; masu-stem + に行く is “what you go to do”.

this.tr: I go to the library.

that.tr: I go to borrow a book.

items.explain: Look at what comes before 「に」: 「図書館」 is a place → destination; 「借り」 is a verb's masu-stem (or an action noun like 「買い物」) → the purpose of going. The two can be combined: 「図書館へ本を借りに行く」.

groups.note: All can mark the place, time or target of an action, and often get the same English translation

items.diff: For destinations, に and へ are mostly interchangeable; に focuses on the “arrival point”, へ on the “direction”. For times and people, only に works.

this.tr: I finally arrived at the station.

that.tr: I'm heading to the station now.

wrong.why: A point in time can only take に

items.explain: Look at the verb: 「着く」「入る」 stress the point of arrival → usually に; 「向かう」「出発する」 only say which way → usually へ; 「行く」「来る」 work with either. Times (７時に) and the target of an action (友達に) can only take に.

items.title: 〜で (place of action)
items.diff: に marks where someone or something “is”; で marks where an action “happens”.

this.tr: There are lots of books in the library.

that.tr: I read books at the library.

wrong.why: The place where an action happens takes で

items.explain: Look at the verb at the end: existing or staying, like 「ある」「いる」「住む」 → に; actions like 「読む」「食べる」「勉強する」 → で. English uses “in / at the library” for both, which is why it's so easy to get wrong.

items.diff: に is exactly at that moment; までに is any time before that moment.

this.tr: Please come at nine tomorrow.

that.tr: Please come by nine tomorrow.

items.explain: The only difference is 「まで」: 「９時に」 is exactly nine o'clock; 「９時までに」 is a deadline — coming at eight or eight-thirty is fine, as long as it's no later than nine.

items.title: 〜と (partner in an action)
items.diff: に means the action is directed one way at the other person; と means both do it together.

this.tr: I told my mom about my worries.

that.tr: For the first time in ages, I had a long chat with my mom.

items.explain: Look at who does what to whom: 「母に話す」 is me telling my mom something — one talks, the other listens; 「母と話す」 is two people talking with each other. For actions that need two people, like 「けんかする」「結婚する」, the partner takes と.

groups.note: Both come from the case particle 「に」 — marking the goal a movement reaches

items.title: 〜に (destination)
items.diff: masu-stem + に行く is “what you go to do”; place + に is “where you go”.

this.tr: I go to borrow a book.

that.tr: I go to the library.

items.explain: Look at what comes before 「に」: 「借り」 is a verb's masu-stem (or an action noun like 「買い物」「散歩」) → the purpose of going; 「図書館」 is a place → destination. The two can be combined: 「図書館へ本を借りに行く」.

groups.note: Both relate to the purpose of “going to do something”

items.diff: に行く can only be followed by “go, come, return”; ために can be followed by any action.

this.tr: I go to the department store to buy clothes.

that.tr: I'm working part-time to buy clothes.

wrong.why: Purpose 「に」 can only be followed by verbs of movement

items.explain: Look at the verb that follows: movement like 「行く」「来る」「帰る」 → masu-stem + に; non-movement actions like 「アルバイトする」「貯金する」 → dictionary form + ために.

items.title: 〜てくる (go and come back)
items.diff: に行く states the purpose of going out; てくる says you'll come back here after taking care of it.

this.tr: Next week I'm going to Kyoto to see temples.

that.tr: I'm just going to grab a drink at the convenience store. Be right back.

items.explain: Look at whether the speaker will come back here: 「ちょっと〜てくるね」 means coming back once done → てくる; 「京都へ見に行く」 only states the purpose of setting off → に行く. The place particles also differ: てくる is often preceded by 「で」 (where you buy it), に行く by 「へ／に」 (where you go).

groups.note: Both express “how often”

items.diff: に〜回 says how many times within a period; おきに says how much is skipped in between — 「１日おき」 = 「２日に１回」.

this.tr: Take this medicine once every two days.

that.tr: Take this medicine every other day.

items.explain: The two sentences mean the same, yet the numbers differ. おきに counts the days left empty in between: １日おき = skipping one day = once every two days, so when you see おきに, add one to the number to get “once every N days”. Expressions of times per day like 「１日に３回」 can only use に〜回.

groups.note: All are used to say “decide on / have something” or “make it into something” — when ordering, making decisions, or changing a state

items.diff: にする follows a noun, mostly when choosing one option out of several; ことにする follows a verb.

this.tr: For my drink, I'll have coffee.

that.tr: For summer vacation, I decided to go to Okinawa.

wrong.why: A verb needs 「こと」 after it

items.explain: First check whether a noun or a verb comes before: コーヒー (noun) → にする; 行く (verb) → ことにする. When ordering food or picking something, 「〜にします」 is the most common.

items.diff: くする／にする is someone “making it” something; くなる／になる is it “becoming” something on its own.

this.tr: I turned down the TV volume.

that.tr: The TV volume got quieter.

items.explain: Look at the particle: 「音を」 → someone adjusts it → くする; 「音が」 → it changed by itself, without saying who did it → くなる. The same goes for decisions: 「会議は月曜日にしました」 means we set it, while 「月曜日になりました」 only reports that it ended up being decided.

items.diff: にする states your own choice and can be used when deciding with friends; をください asks a staff member for something.

this.tr: I'll have the curry.

that.tr: Excuse me, the curry, please.

items.explain: Look at who you're talking to: looking at the menu with friends and saying what you'll pick → にする (「何にする？」「カレーにする」); asking a staff member for something → をください. Saying 「カレーにします」 to staff is also fine, but saying 「カレーをください」 to a friend turns into “please give me curry”.

groups.note: Both come from 「〜が好き・〜が上手」 — the object of 「好き」「上手」 is marked with 「が」 and must be a noun, so a verb first needs 「の」

items.diff: To like a thing, use “noun + が好き”; to like doing something, first add 「の」: “verb + のが好き”.

this.tr: I like listening to music.

that.tr: I like music.

wrong.why: A verb can't attach directly to 「が好き」 — add 「の」

items.explain: Look at what comes before 「が好き」: 音楽 is a noun → attaches directly; 聞く is a verb → first add 「の」 to turn it into a noun. Since English says “I like…” for both, the 「の」 is easy to leave out.

groups.note: Both can turn a verb into a noun

items.diff: Before liking or being good at something, の and こと mostly both work; to state content at the end of a sentence, like 「趣味は〜」, only こと works.

this.tr: I like reading books.

that.tr: My hobby is reading books.

wrong.why: To state content with 「〜は〜ことです」, only こと works

items.explain: Before 「好き」「上手」, の is the most natural; こと also works but sounds more literary. When stating the content of a hobby or dream with 「〜は〜ことです」, only こと works — with の it becomes the explanatory 「のです」, and the meaning is wrong.

groups.note: Both come from the position word 「前（まえ）」 — originally “in front” in space, and borrowed for time as “before” when attached to an action

items.diff: の前 follows a place and means “in front of” in space; 前に follows an action or activity and means “before” in time.

this.tr: I waited for my friend in front of the station.

that.tr: Before getting on the train, I bought a ticket.

wrong.why: A verb attaches directly to 「前に」 without 「の」

items.explain: Look at the word before 「前」: places or objects like 駅 or 家 → position in space, “in front of…”; a verb like 乗る, or an activity noun like 食事 or 授業 plus 「の」 → time, “before…”. Don't add 「の」 after a verb.

groups.note: の中（なか） ↔ 中（じゅう） — the same kanji 「中」, but different readings and meanings

items.title: 〜中（じゅう）
items.diff: の中（なか） is the “inside” of something; 「中」 attached directly to a noun is read じゅう and means “all through / the whole…”.

this.tr: There's a cat in the box.

that.tr: It rained all day long.

items.explain: Look at whether 「の」 comes before 「中」: with 「の」 → read なか, meaning the inside of a space; attached directly to a time or place noun (一日中, 世界中) → read じゅう, meaning “throughout, all of”.

groups.note: Both are comparison patterns

items.diff: For three or more, use 「の中で〜が一番」; with only two, ask 「どちらが」.

this.tr: Of all fruits, which do you like best?

that.tr: Apples or mandarins — which do you like more?

items.explain: Count what's being compared: 「果物」 is a whole category with three or more → の中で〜が一番, and ask with 「何／どれ」; only two things, りんご and みかん → AとBとどちらが, and answer with 「〜のほうが」.

items.diff: の中で〜が一番 picks the top one from a group; より〜のほうが compares two, with B beating A.

this.tr: Of all sports, I like soccer the most.

that.tr: I like soccer more than baseball.

items.explain: Look at how many things are compared: 「スポーツの中で」 draws a circle around a whole category → 一番 (most); 「野球より」 compares with just one → のほうが (more).

groups.note: When modifying nouns, marking subjects, or turning clauses into nouns, these share the same job as 「の」

items.diff: A noun modifying a noun needs 「の」; verbs and i-adjectives modify nouns directly, without 「の」.

this.tr: This is my book.

that.tr: This is the book I bought yesterday.

wrong.why: Don't add 「の」 when a verb modifies a noun

items.explain: Look at what kind of word does the modifying: nouns like 私 or 日本 → add 「の」; verbs and i-adjectives like 買った, 行く, 高い → attach directly to the noun. Learners who think of の as “of / 's” often add an extra 「の」 after verbs too.

items.diff: A noun modifying a noun uses 「の」; a na-adjective modifying a noun uses 「な」.

this.tr: This is a Japanese car.

that.tr: This is a beautiful car.

wrong.why: A na-adjective modifying a noun uses 「な」

items.explain: First decide whether the word before is a noun or a na-adjective: 日本 and 学校 are nouns → の; きれい, 静か, 有名 are na-adjectives → な. Although 「きれい」 ends in 「い」, it's a na-adjective, and is the one most often wrongly written as 「きれいの」.

items.title: 〜が (subject)
items.diff: In a clause modifying a noun, the subject can take 「の」 instead of 「が」; the subject of the whole sentence can only take 「が」.

this.tag: In a clause · の = が
this.tr: This is a dish my mom made.

that.tr: My mom made a dish.

items.explain: Look at whether a modified noun follows: in 「母の作った料理」, 「作った」 modifies 「料理」, so the 「の」 here equals 「が」; if the sentence ends at 「作った」 with no noun after it → only 「が」 works.

items.diff: Both can turn a clause into a noun; for a scene you directly see or hear, only 「の」 works, and with 「〜ことができる」 only 「こと」 works.

this.tr: I can hear birds singing.

that.tr: I can play the piano.

wrong.why: Only 「の」 can come before perception verbs

items.explain: Look at the final verb: with perception verbs like 「見える」「聞こえる」「見る」, what comes before is a concrete scene happening in front of you → の; abstract expressions like 「できる」 or 「趣味は〜です」 → こと. Before 「好き」「上手」, either works.

groups.note: Both come from 「の + だ」 — presenting what comes before as a fact

items.diff: ので sits mid-sentence and must be followed by a result; んです ends the sentence and explains the situation on its own.

this.tr: I have a headache, so I'll go home early today.

that.tr: Sorry, it's just that I have a headache.

items.explain: Look at whether the sentence is finished: ので is always followed by another clause (早く帰ります); んです ends the sentence, used to answer 「どうしたんですか」 or to explain your situation to someone.

groups.note: Both express a reason, “because…”

items.title: 〜から (reason)
items.diff: ので presents the reason as an objective fact and sounds softer; から is the speaker's subjective reason, and only から works in 「〜からです」 at the end of a sentence.

this.tr: Excuse me, I have a fever — may I go home early?

that.tr: The reason I took yesterday off is that I had a fever.

wrong.why: To give the reason at the end of a sentence, only 「からです」 works

items.explain: Check two things: when making a request to a boss or teacher, ので sounds objective rather than like an excuse; when you state the result first and add the reason at the end (〜のは〜からです), only から works.

items.title: 〜て (reason)
items.diff: ので can be followed by a request or intention; て, when giving a reason, can only be followed by a feeling or an uncontrollable result.

this.tr: We're out of time, so please hurry.

that.tr: I had no time, and I was in a bind.

wrong.why: A reason 「て」 can't be followed by a request

items.explain: Look at the second half: requests or intentions like 「〜てください」「〜ましょう」 → only ので (or から); feelings or natural results like 「困った」「びっくりした」 → て works.

groups.note: Both modify nouns, and English often renders them as “noun + of / 's” or a relative clause

items.diff: Verbs and i-adjectives modify nouns directly; only a noun modifying a noun takes 「の」.

this.tr: This is the book I bought yesterday.

that.tr: This is my book.

wrong.why: Don't add 「の」 when a verb modifies a noun

items.explain: Look at what kind of word does the modifying: verbs and i-adjectives like 買った, 読む, 高い → go straight before the noun; nouns like 私 or 日本 → add 「の」. Learners who think of の as a general linking word often write ✗買ったの本 or ✗高いの本.

groups.note: All come from “question word + particle” — か (question → an uncertain “some…”), も (also → “all / (not) any”), でも (even → “any… at all”)

items.diff: question word + か is “something / some…”; question word + も + negative is “not a single one”.

this.tr: Is there anything in the fridge?

that.tr: There's nothing in the fridge.

wrong.why: 「何も」 must be followed by a negative

items.explain: Look at the kana after the question word and the end of the sentence: 「何か」 can be followed by a statement or a question and means “something”; 「何も」 is always followed by a negative (ない) and means “nothing at all”. When asked 「何かある？」, if there's nothing, answer 「何もない」.

items.title: Question word + でも
items.diff: question word + か is “some one” (unspecified); question word + でも is “any one is fine” (all of them).

this.tr: I'm hungry. I want to eat something.

that.tr: I'm hungry. I want to eat — anything will do.

items.explain: Look at what follows: 何か means “something”, without saying what; 何でも is often followed by 「いい」, meaning “anything is fine”. Note the readings: 何か is read なにか, 何でも is read なんでも.

groups.note: All come from “question word + particle” — か (question → an uncertain “some…”), も (also → “all / (not) any”), でも (even → “any… at all”)

items.diff: question word + も + negative is “not a single one”; question word + か is “something / some…”.

this.tr: There's nothing in the fridge.

that.tr: Is there anything in the fridge?

wrong.why: 「何も」 must be followed by a negative

items.explain: Look at the kana after the question word and the end of the sentence: 「何も」 is always followed by a negative (ない) and means “nothing at all”; 「何か」 can be followed by a statement or a question and means “something”. When asked 「何かある？」, if there's nothing, answer 「何もない」.

items.title: Question word + でも
items.diff: 何も + negative is “nothing”; 何でも + affirmative is “anything / everything”.

this.tr: I don't feel like eating anything today.

that.tr: I can eat anything.

items.explain: Look at the end of the sentence: negative → 何も (negating everything); affirmative → 何でも (affirming everything). The readings differ too: 何も is read なにも, 何でも is read なんでも.

groups.note: Both mean “not at all”

items.diff: 何も〜ない negates “things” — not a single thing; 全然〜ない negates “degree” — not at all.

this.tr: I haven't eaten anything since this morning.

that.tr: I haven't been eating vegetables at all lately.

items.explain: Look at whether there's an object: 何も itself takes the place of 「を」, so the food doesn't appear in the sentence; 全然 is an adverb, so it can go with 「野菜を」, and can also modify adjectives (全然おいしくない) — 何も can't.

groups.note: Both mean “only…”

items.diff: だけ objectively says “only”, and works with affirmative or negative; しか must be followed by a negative and carries a sense of “too little, not enough”.

this.tr: I've only got 1,000 yen left in my wallet.

that.tr: There's just 1,000 yen in my wallet.

wrong.why: 「しか」 must always be followed by a negative

items.explain: Look at the end of the sentence: しか is always followed by a negative (ない, 〜ません), the speaker feels it's too little, and it often goes with 「もう」; だけ can be followed by an affirmative and simply states the amount.

items.diff: しか〜ない means nothing other than that; ばかり means “nothing but, always”, other things may exist too, and it often sounds disapproving.

this.tr: My brother eats only meat (nothing else).

that.tr: My brother eats nothing but meat.

items.explain: しか〜ない excludes everything else, stressing “only this”; ばかり says there's too much or too often of something, often with criticism, and is followed by an affirmative (食べている). Both can be translated “only eats meat”, but you can tell them apart by whether the sentence ends negative or affirmative.

groups.note: All express contrast, “but”

items.title: でも (sentence-initial: but)
items.diff: しかし is literary, used in writing and speeches; でも is conversational, used in everyday chat.

this.tr: The exam was difficult. However, everyone passed.

that.tr: The exam was so hard. But everyone passed!

items.explain: Look at the overall tone: chatting with 「よ」「ね」 at the end and words like 「みんな」 → でも; written style like reports, news or essays → しかし. Saying 「しかし」 when chatting with friends sounds stiff.

items.diff: けど sits mid-sentence, attached right after the first clause; しかし goes at the start of a new sentence.

this.tr: This restaurant is expensive. But the food is delicious.

that.tr: This restaurant is expensive, but the food is delicious.

wrong.why: しかし is a stand-alone conjunction — end the previous sentence with a period first

items.explain: Look at the position: right after the first clause → けど (けれども); after the sentence has been ended with 「。」, at the start of a new sentence → しかし.

items.diff: しかし is a general contrast; ところが is used specifically when the outcome is unexpected.

this.tr: This plan is good. However, it costs too much.

that.tr: I rushed over there. But, to my surprise, the shop was already closed.

items.explain: Look at the second half: giving your own view or raising a problem → しかし; telling something that already happened, contrary to expectations (usually past tense) → ところが. ところが can't be followed by your own opinion or a request.

groups.note: All can mean “and then / also”

items.diff: それから is mostly spoken, adding “one more thing”; そして is mostly for description or narration, adding smoothly, and feels slightly more literary.

this.tr: Two coffees, please. Oh, and one piece of cake too.

that.tr: This town is quiet. And it's very beautiful.

items.explain: Look at the situation: ordering or giving instructions and remembering “one more thing” → それから; describing another feature of the same thing, or the next step in a story → そして. For “after that / since then”, only それから works.

items.diff: それから is just “one more thing”; それに adds another point to a reason or evaluation: “what's more”.

this.tr: Pick up some milk for me. Oh, and eggs too, please.

that.tr: Let's go with this room. It's spacious, and what's more, it's close to the station.

items.explain: Look at what's being added: one more errand or item to buy → それから; one more merit or reason to persuade someone → それに, often used with 「〜し」.

items.diff: てから links “A first, then B” within one sentence; それから goes at the start of a sentence and links two sentences.

this.tr: First I'll do my homework. Then I'll play.

that.tr: I'll play after doing my homework.

items.explain: Same meaning; look at the position: a verb directly followed by 「てから」 → said in one sentence; split with 「。」 and starting the next with 「それから」 → two sentences. それから is common when you're thinking as you talk, or listing things one by one.

groups.note: All can link two events or facts

items.diff: そして smoothly adds or narrates the next step, and feels slightly more literary; それから is mostly spoken, adding “one more thing”.

this.tr: This town is quiet. And it's very beautiful.

that.tr: Two coffees, please. Oh, and one piece of cake too.

items.explain: Look at the situation: describing another feature of the same thing, or the next step in a story → そして; ordering or giving instructions and remembering “one more thing” → それから. For “after that / since then”, only それから works.

items.title: 〜て (sequence of actions)
items.diff: Consecutive actions within one sentence are linked with て; そして goes at the start of a sentence, where a pause is wanted.

this.tr: I ate breakfast. And then I went to school.

that.tr: I ate breakfast and went to school.

items.explain: Both mean the same; look at the period: for several actions done in a row by the same person, linking them with the te-form in one sentence is most natural; そして needs a 「。」 before it and suits writing that stresses “next”. Linking every action with 「〜た。そして、」 reads very stiffly.

items.diff: そして adds smoothly; それに adds one more point to a reason, and is more conversational.

this.tr: He's kind. And he's smart, too.

that.tr: I'm not going today. It's raining, and besides, I'm tired.

items.explain: Look at whether reasons are being given: just introducing features of a person or thing → そして; piling up reasons one by one to explain “why”, often with 「〜し」 → それに.

items.diff: そして only means something happened next; それで clearly marks the first part as the cause and the second as the result.

this.tr: I opened the door. Then I went inside.

that.tr: The rain got heavier. So the match was called off.

items.explain: Look at whether there's cause and effect: “open the door → go in” is just the order of actions → そして; “the rain got heavier” is the cause of “the match was called off” → それで. そして itself doesn't carry the meaning of “so”.

groups.note: Both express the time order “do B after finishing A”

items.diff: たあとで only expresses time order; てから can also mean “ever since…”.

this.tr: After watching a movie, I had a meal.

that.tr: It's already been three years since I came to Japan.

wrong.why: “Ever since…” can only take てから

items.explain: Look at the second half: if it says how much time has passed (もう３年になる), or how things have been since then → only てから. If it just gives the order of two actions, both work: たあとで regardless of the gap in between, while てから stresses “finish A first, then do B”.

groups.note: Both can express that something has happened or been completed, and often get the same English translation

items.diff: た says the event happened; ている says the state left by that event still holds now.

this.tr: My brother got married last year.

that.tr: My brother is already married.

items.explain: Look at the time words: 「去年」 pins down when it happened → た; no specific time, talking about the present state (married, where someone lives, who someone knows) → ている. English sometimes blurs “got married” and “is married”; Japanese makes you choose between “the event” and “the current state”.

items.diff: た is the plain past; ました is the polite past — same meaning.

this.tr: Yesterday I saw a movie with a friend.

that.tr: Sensei, yesterday I saw a movie with a friend.

wrong.why: You can't just add 「です」 after a verb's ta-form — use 「ました」

items.explain: Look at who you're talking to: friends, family, a diary → た; teachers, bosses, people you don't know well → ました. To be polite, replace 「見た」 entirely with 「見ました」 — don't add 「です」 after it.

groups.note: Both come from 「こと + がある」 — “there is such a thing”

items.diff: ta-form + ことがある is “have done… before”; dictionary form + ことがある is “sometimes…”.

this.tr: When I was a kid, I was late for school once or twice.

that.tr: Even now, I'm occasionally late for work.

items.explain: The only difference is 「た」 vs. 「る」: ta-form → a past experience, often with 「子どもの時」「一度」; dictionary form → something that occasionally happens now, often with 「たまに」「時々」.

groups.note: Both talk about the past

items.diff: た says what you did at a certain time; たことがある says whether you've ever had that experience in your life.

this.tr: I've climbed Mt. Fuji once.

that.tr: I climbed Mt. Fuji yesterday.

wrong.why: With a specific time, use 「た」

items.explain: Look at the time words: a specific time like 「昨日」「先週」 → just reporting that event, use た; words about experience like 「一度」「今まで」「子どもの時」 → たことがある.

groups.note: Both mark plurals, “… and others / these…”

items.diff: たち in principle only attaches to people; ら can also attach to words for things like 「これ・それ」.

this.tr: The children are playing in the park.

that.tr: Please read these documents.

wrong.why: 「たち」 only attaches to people (or animals treated like people)

items.explain: Look at what it attaches to: people (私, 子ども, 学生) → たち is the most common; words for things like これ, それ → only ら works. ら with people (僕ら, 彼ら) is more casual than たち; use たち in polite settings.

groups.note: Both come from 「たい」 — expressing an inner wish to do something

items.diff: たい says you yourself want to do something; たがる says someone else seems to want to.

this.tr: I want to buy a new game.

that.tr: My little brother wants to buy a new game.

items.explain: Look at the subject: I (or “you” in a question) → たい; third parties like a brother or friend → you can't see inside their mind, only describe how they appear → たがっている (usually in the ている form).

groups.note: All express “want”

items.diff: たい attaches to verbs — wanting to do an action; ほしい attaches to nouns — wanting a thing.

this.tr: I want to buy a new car.

that.tr: I want a new car.

wrong.why: After a verb, use 「たい」

items.explain: Look at what follows “want”: an action (買う) → masu-stem + たい; a thing (車) → がほしい. Watch the particle too: ほしい takes 「が」 before it.

items.diff: たい is wanting to do something yourself; てほしい is wanting someone else to do it.

this.tr: I want to go home early today.

that.tr: I want my husband to come home early today.

items.explain: Look at who does the action: yourself → たい; wanting the listener or someone else to do it → “person に + te-form + ほしい” (夫に〜てほしい). Both may be “want” in English, but “want someone to…” needs てほしい.

items.diff: たい is just a wish and may not come true; つもりだ is a plan already made.

this.tr: Someday I want to study abroad in Japan.

that.tr: I plan to go study in Japan next spring.

items.explain: Look at how specific the time is: a vague future like 「いつか」 → just a wish (たい); a set time like 「来年の春」 → an existing plan (つもりだ). They attach differently too: たい to the masu-stem, つもり to the dictionary form.

groups.note: Both can list several things side by side

items.title: 〜て (sequence of actions)
items.diff: たり〜たり just gives a few examples, in no particular order; て links actions one by one in the order they actually happened.

this.tr: On Sundays I do things like laundry and cleaning.

that.tr: This morning I did the laundry, then cleaned.

items.explain: Look at the time words: 「日曜日は」 talks about what you usually do, picking a few examples among others → たり〜たり; 「今朝は」 talks about what you actually did, linked in order → て. With たり, don't forget the final 「する」.

items.diff: たり〜たり lists actions (verbs); や〜など lists things (nouns).

this.tr: On weekends I do things like reading and watching movies.

that.tr: My bag has books, notebooks and so on in it.

items.explain: Look at what's being listed: actions like reading or watching movies → たり〜たりする; things like books or notebooks → や〜など. English uses “things like… and so on” for both, but Japanese makes you distinguish verbs from nouns.

groups.note: All can link two actions or two events

items.diff: て just links in order; てから stresses “finish A first, and only then do B”.

this.tr: Yesterday I got home, took a shower and went to bed.

that.tr: Be sure to wash your hands before you eat.

items.explain: Look at what the sentence is doing: narrating a series of things you did → て; stressing that the order can't be reversed, a “first A, then B” rule or procedure → てから, often with 「必ず」「まず」. The “ever since” meaning, as in 「日本に来てから３年」, also only works with てから.

items.diff: て links actions one by one in the order they actually happened; たり〜たり just gives a few examples, in no particular order.

this.tr: This morning I did the laundry, then cleaned.

that.tr: On Sundays I do things like laundry and cleaning.

items.explain: Look at the time words: 「今朝は」 talks about what you actually did, linked in order → て; 「日曜日は」 talks about what you usually do, picking a few examples among others → たり〜たり.

items.diff: て, when giving a reason, can only be followed by a feeling or an uncontrollable result; ので can be followed by a request or intention.

this.tr: I had no time, and I was in a bind.

that.tr: We're out of time, so please hurry.

wrong.why: A reason 「て」 can't be followed by a request

items.explain: Look at the second half: feelings or natural results like 「困った」「びっくりした」 → て works; requests or intentions like 「〜てください」「〜ましょう」 → use ので (or から).

items.diff: て expresses the posture or manner in which the second action is done; ながら is doing two separate things at the same time.

this.tr: I read a book sitting in a chair.

that.tr: I read a book while listening to music.

items.explain: Look at whether the first part is another action “in progress”: 「座る」 is a posture kept after sitting down → て (座って, 立って, 眼鏡をかけて); 「聞く」 is another action going on alongside reading → ながら. English may use “-ing” for both.

groups.note: ている ↔ てある — just one character apart

items.diff: ている (with intransitive verbs) only describes a state; てある (with transitive verbs) means someone deliberately did it and the result remains.

this.tr: The window is open.

that.tr: The window has been opened (by someone) for the cleaning.

wrong.why: After 「窓が」, use 「開いている」 or 「開けてある」

items.explain: First look at the verb: 開く (intransitive) + ている → just “is open”; 開ける (transitive) + てある → someone opened it for a purpose and left it open. If you see a purpose like 「〜のために」, it's most likely てある.

groups.note: All can express an action in progress, a continuing state, or completion

items.diff: ている describes the current state; た says the event happened at a certain time.

this.tr: My brother is already married.

that.tr: My brother got married last year.

items.explain: Look at the time words: no specific time, talking about the present state (married, where someone lives, who someone knows) → ている; 「去年」 pins down when it happened → た.

items.title: 〜ているところだ
items.diff: ている can also express habits; ているところだ only means “right in the middle of it now”.

this.tr: My dad reads the newspaper every morning.

that.tr: My dad is reading the newspaper right now.

items.explain: Look at the time words: 「毎朝」「いつも」 → a habit, only ている works; 「今」「ちょうど」 → in progress at this moment, and ているところだ makes it clearer — often used to answer 「今、何をしているの？」.

items.diff: ている describes a state at the end of a sentence; たまま means doing something else while keeping a certain state.

this.tr: He has his shoes on.

that.tr: He went into the room with his shoes still on.

items.explain: Look at whether another action follows: the state itself is the point and the sentence ends → ている; doing something else in that state (入った, 寝た), often implying “that shouldn't be done” → たまま. English may use “with… on” for both.

groups.note: All come from 「てから」 — “from the moment … is done”

items.diff: てから only says “A first, then B”; てからでないと says “unless A is done first, B can't happen”.

this.tr: I'll get back to you after I check.

that.tr: I can't give you an answer until I've checked.

items.explain: Look at the second half: an ordinary next action (返事します) → てから, just ordering things; a negative like 「できない」「わからない」 → てからでないと, stressing that A is an essential precondition.

items.diff: てから is an ordinary “since…”; てからというもの is literary and stresses a big, lasting change since then.

this.tr: It's already been three years since I came to Japan.

that.tr: Ever since our child was born, every day has been incredibly busy.

items.explain: てからというもの is followed by a marked change that has continued “ever since”, with strong feeling, mostly in writing; if you're just saying how much time has passed (３年になる), use ordinary てから.

groups.note: し・て・から ↔ し・た・から: just て vs. た — one means “after”, the other “because”

items.title: 〜から (reason)
items.diff: te-form + から is “after doing…”; ta-form + から is “because…”.

this.tr: I'll go play after I finish my homework.

that.tr: I've already done my homework, so I can go play.

items.explain: Just one kana apart: し・て・から is time order, followed by the next thing to do; し・た・から is a reason, followed by the resulting outcome or judgment (行ける, 大丈夫だ).

groups.note: Both express “first…, then…”

items.diff: たあとで only says B happens after A; てから can also mean “ever since…”, followed by elapsed time or a continuing state.

this.tr: It's already been half a year since I started learning Japanese.

that.tr: After class ended, I went to ask the teacher a question.

wrong.why: “It's been … since…” can only take てから

items.explain: Look at the second half: time or a state continuing from then on, like 「もう半年になる」「ずっと〜」 → only てから; just saying the next thing happened afterwards → both たあとで and てから work. Note how they attach: te-form + から, ta-form + あとで.

items.title: 〜て (sequence of actions)
items.diff: て just strings several actions together in order; てから stresses “finish A first, and only then do B”.

this.tr: Wash your hands first, then eat.

that.tr: In the morning I get up, wash my face and eat breakfast.

items.explain: A series of everyday actions done in order → link them one after another with て; to stress “finish A first, B has to wait until after A”, often with 「まず」 → てから, which usually links just two actions.

groups.note: Both come from 「ください」 — the imperative of 「くださる」 (to give me)

items.diff: te-form + ください asks someone to “do” something; noun + をください asks someone to “give” something.

this.tr: Excuse me, could you bring me a glass of water?

that.tr: Excuse me, water, please.

items.explain: Look at what comes before ください: a verb's te-form (持ってきて) → asking someone to do that action; noun + を (水を) → asking someone to give you that thing. When shopping or ordering, use をください.

items.diff: てください is an ordinary request; お〜ください is the honorific form used with customers, and is more respectful.

this.tr: Please wait a moment.

that.tr: We apologize, but please wait a moment.

items.explain: Look at the form and setting: お + masu-stem (待ち) + ください, often with 「少々」「恐れ入りますが」, appears in shops, announcements and notices; between friends or coworkers, 「待ってください」 is enough.

groups.note: All ask someone to do something

items.diff: てください is a polite instruction that the listener basically can't refuse; ていただけませんか uses a question to leave the decision to the listener, and is softer.

this.tr: Please write your name here.

that.tr: Sorry to bother you when you're busy, but could you write your name here?

items.explain: Look at who you're asking and the tone: instructions from a service counter or teacher → てください; asking a superior or client to do something extra for you, often after 「お忙しいところすみませんが」 → ていただけませんか.

items.diff: てください is a polite request; なさい is a command from someone higher to someone lower.

this.tr: It's getting late, so please get some rest early.

that.tr: It's already ten! Go to bed now!

items.explain: Look at the relationship between speakers: parent to child, teacher to student → なさい, never to equals or superiors; a polite request to people in general → てください. They attach differently too: なさい follows the masu-stem (寝なさい, 書きなさい).

groups.note: Both come from 「ても + いい」 — “it's fine even if…”: fine to do it = may; fine not to = needn't

items.diff: てもいい is “you may do it”; なくてもいい is “you don't have to do it”.

this.tr: You can come tomorrow, you know.

that.tr: You don't have to come tomorrow, you know.

items.explain: Look at what comes before て: an affirmative te-form (来て) → permission to do it; the negative 「なくて」 (来なくて) → it's fine not to, i.e. “needn't” — the opposite of 「来なければならない」 (must come).

groups.note: Both express permission, “may… / it's fine if…”

items.diff: Both express permission; てもかまわない is more formal, used mostly with customers and in business.

this.tr: You can pay next month, no problem.

that.tr: It's perfectly fine to make your payment next month.

items.explain: Same meaning; look at the setting: between friends, casually with 「よ」 → てもいい; staff to customers or in business, often with honorifics like 「お支払い」 → てもかまいません, which sounds more formal.

groups.note: Both come from 「いけない」 (no good) — doing it is no good = forbidden; not doing it is no good = must

items.diff: てはいけない is “doing it is no good” = must not; ないといけない is “not doing it is no good” = must.

this.tr: You're not allowed to use English in this class.

that.tr: You have to use Japanese in this class.

items.explain: Look at the condition before いけない: affirmative 「使っては」 (if you use it) → no good = forbidden; negative 「使わないと」 (if you don't use it) → no good = must.

groups.note: All express prohibition, “don't / must not”

items.diff: Both express prohibition; てはならない is used in laws, maxims and writing, and sounds more solemn.

this.tr: You're not allowed to chew gum in the classroom.

that.tr: Whatever the reason, you must never hurt others.

items.explain: Look at the setting and topic: everyday rules at school or work → てはいけない; laws, maxims, speeches laying down principles → てはならない, which is rare in everyday conversation.

items.diff: てはいけない announces a rule; ないでください asks someone not to do something, and is more polite.

this.tr: This is a non-smoking area. Smoking is not allowed.

that.tr: Excuse me, please don't smoke here.

items.explain: てはいけない passes judgment from the standpoint of a rule, so saying it to a customer's or superior's face sounds like a scolding; ないでください makes a request of the listener and sounds gentle. When asking someone in person to stop, ないでください is usually used.

items.title: 〜な (prohibition)
items.diff: てはいけない explains a rule; verb dictionary form + な is a very blunt command-style prohibition.

this.tr: It's dangerous, so you mustn't swim in the river.

that.tr: Danger! Don't swim in the river!

items.explain: Look at the end of the sentence: 「な」 attached directly to the dictionary form (泳ぐな) is a command-style prohibition, used on signs, in angry scolding or in men's casual speech, and is very rude said to someone; てはいけない reasons with someone or states a rule, and isn't as harsh.

groups.note: Both are used for comparison

items.diff: どちらが is used to ask “which is more…”; より〜のほうが is used to answer “… is more…”.

this.tr: Dogs or cats — which do you like more?

that.tr: I like cats more than dogs.

items.explain: When asking, set the two options side by side with 「と」 and follow with 「どちらが」; when answering, mark the losing side with 「より」 and the winning side with 「のほうが」 — don't answer ✗犬と猫と猫のほうが好きです.

items.diff: どちら is only used between two things; for three or more, use 「の中で〜がいちばん」.

this.tr: Apples or mandarins — which do you like more?

that.tag: Three or more → いちばん
that.tr: Of all fruits, which do you like best?

items.explain: First count the options: only two (りんごとみかん) → どちらが; three or more within a range (果物の中で) → use 「何／どれ／誰が いちばん」.

groups.note: All come from 「と + 言う」 — originally “to be called… / to say…”

items.diff: という is followed by a noun and means “(a person, thing) called…”; と言う is the predicate and means “(someone) said…”.

this.tr: A man named Tanaka called just now.

that.tr: Mr. Tanaka said he'd come tomorrow.

items.explain: Look at what follows 「と」: a noun (人, 店, 本) → introducing a name, usually written in kana as 「という」; the sentence ends at 「言いました」 → quoting someone, usually written with the kanji 「言う」.

items.diff: という is followed by a noun and introduces a name; というのは takes a word as the topic and then explains its meaning.

this.tr: Do you know the word 「スマホ」?

that.tr: 「スマホ」 means a smartphone.

items.explain: Look at what follows: 「という + noun (言葉, 人)」 just attaches a name to the noun; 「というのは」 is followed by an explanation of it, often ending in 「〜のことです」「〜という意味です」.

groups.note: All come from quotative 「と」 + 「言う」 (って is the spoken contraction of 「と言って」)

items.diff: と言う is the predicate and means “(someone) said…”; という is followed by a noun and means “(a person, thing) called…”.

this.tr: Mr. Tanaka said he'd come tomorrow.

that.tr: A man named Tanaka called just now.

items.explain: Look at what follows 「と」: the sentence ends at 「言いました」 → quoting someone, usually written with the kanji 「言う」; a noun (人, 店, 本) → introducing a name, usually written in kana as 「という」.

items.diff: と言いました narrates what was said at the time; と言っていました passes on a third person's words to the listener.

this.tr: At the meeting, the manager said, “Let's give it our best.”

that.tr: The manager said tomorrow's meeting is canceled.

items.explain: Look at the purpose: recounting who said what in a scene → と言いました; passing someone's words on to the listener, “that's what he said” → と言っていました, often ending with 「よ」.

items.title: 〜って (reported speech at sentence end)
items.diff: と言っていました is a full, polite way to report; sentence-final って is a casual shortened form.

this.tr: The teacher said tomorrow is a day off.

that.tr: Hey, I heard tomorrow's a day off.

items.explain: って can replace 「と」, and at the end of a sentence it can also drop 「言っていた」, meaning “I heard…”; it's only used with friends and family. With teachers, bosses or in formal settings, say the full 「と言っていました」.

groups.note: All are 「と + 思う」 — quoting what's in your mind

items.diff: plain form + と思う is a guess or opinion; volitional form + と思う is your own intention.

this.tr: I think Mr. Tanaka will go tomorrow.

that.tr: I'm thinking of going tomorrow.

items.explain: The only difference is 「行く」 vs. 「行こう」: plain form (行く) → a guess or opinion about something; volitional form (行こう) → the speaker's own intention to do it.

items.diff: と思う is the speaker's thought at this moment; と思っている is a thought held over time, and can also describe someone else's thoughts.

this.tr: I'd like to study abroad.

that.tr: My brother has long wanted to study abroad.

items.explain: Look at the subject: your own current thought → と思う; a third person's (兄, 彼) thoughts, or your own long-held thoughts → と思っている. 「兄は〜と思います」 would be understood as “I think my brother…”, which changes the meaning.

groups.note: Both express a guess

items.diff: と思う carries the speaker's personal view; でしょう sounds objective and is common in weather forecasts.

this.tr: I think it'll rain tomorrow.

that.tr: Tomorrow, rain is expected across most of the country.

wrong.why: A noun needs 「だ」 after it: 雨だと思います

items.explain: と思う is “I think”, suited to giving your own view in conversation; でしょう doesn't put “I” forward, making an objective guess like a weather forecast. Note how they attach: after a noun, と思う needs 「だ」 (雨だと思う), while でしょう attaches directly (雨でしょう).

groups.note: Both can be rendered in English as “the same as / like…”

items.title: 〜ように (simile)
items.diff: と同じ means actually “the same”; のように is “like…”, and can be followed by adjectives or verbs.

this.tr: My sister graduated from the same university as my mom.

that.tr: My sister is kind, just like my mom.

wrong.why: 同じ can't directly modify an adjective

items.explain: Look at what follows 「同じ」: a noun (大学, 色) or 「だ」 → the two really are the same; to say “(kind, pretty) just like…”, followed by an adjective or verb → use のように. Thinking “the same as” for both leads to ✗母と同じ優しい.

groups.note: と has several jobs, each with a similar alternative: “and” ≈ や, “as soon as / when” ≈ たら, “the person you meet” ≈ に

items.diff: と lists everything; や〜など only gives a few examples, implying there are others.

this.tr: There's a book and a notebook in my bag (just those two).

that.tr: There are books, notebooks and so on in my bag.

items.explain: The two sentences differ only in the particle: what と lists is everything; や (often with など) just picks a few representatives, and there are other things in the bag.

items.diff: と can only be followed by something that naturally happens; たら can also be followed by a request or intention.

this.tr: When you get to the station, there's a bank right in front of you.

that.tr: When you get to the station, please give me a call.

wrong.why: と can't be followed by a request or command

items.explain: The first halves are the same; look at the second half: directions, machine operations, natural laws — “once A happens, B appears” → と; a request or intention like 「てください」「〜たい」「〜よう」 → only たら.

items.title: 〜に (target of an action)
items.diff: と means both sides do it together; に means it's directed one way toward the other person.

this.tr: On the weekend I met up with a friend and we had a meal together.

that.tr: I happened to run into my teacher at the station.

wrong.why: 結婚する requires both people, so the partner takes 「と」

items.explain: 「会う」 works with both: meeting by arrangement, seeing each other → と; going to see someone yourself, or bumping into them → に. Actions that only work with two people together, like 「結婚する」「けんかする」, can only take と.

groups.note: All can express “when…”

items.diff: とき only states the time; たら carries a condition, “once… happens, then…”.

this.tr: When I went to Japan last year, I climbed Mt. Fuji.

that.tr: When I go to Japan next time, I want to climb Mt. Fuji.

items.explain: Look at the time words and the end of the sentence: 「去年」 + a past fact → とき, just stating when; 「今度」 + an intention or request like 「〜たい」「〜てください」 → usually たら, meaning “once A happens, do B”.

items.diff: とき is a point or period in time; 間 is a whole stretch of time, often used with 「ずっと」.

this.tr: During summer vacation, I went back to my home country once.

that.tr: I stayed in my home country for the whole summer vacation.

items.explain: Look at the second half: a state lasting through the whole period, like 「ずっと〜ていた」 → 間; a single event that happened during that time (一度帰った) → とき.

items.diff: とき refers to an actual time; 場合は refers to a hypothetical situation, mostly in rules and instructions.

this.tr: When I was a kid, I often played in this river.

that.tr: In case of fire, please do not use the elevator.

items.explain: 場合は means “in the event of…”, used in rules, manuals and notices about hypothetical situations that haven't happened, with a formal tone; things that already happened, or a period of life (子どものとき), can only take とき.

groups.note: All express “intend / plan”

items.diff: (よ)うと思う is mostly an idea that just came up while speaking; つもりだ is a firmer plan decided long ago.

this.tr: I've been planning for a while to study abroad next year.

that.tr: It's raining, so I think I'll take a taxi home today.

items.explain: Look at when it was decided: thought of on the spot after seeing the rain → (よ)うと思う; a plan settled long ago and being prepared for (前から) → つもりだ.

items.diff: つもり is a personal intention in your mind; 予定 is an already-arranged schedule.

this.tr: I'm planning to go back to my home country over summer vacation.

that.tr: The plane is scheduled to arrive at three.

wrong.why: A plane has no “intentions” — use 予定 for schedules

items.explain: Look at the subject: a person's own thoughts → つもり; already-arranged schedules like flights, meetings or events, or arrangements set by a company or others → 予定.

items.diff: つもりだ is an intention you've had in mind; ことにした is the moment you make up your mind.

this.tr: I plan to study abroad next year.

that.tr: I went back and forth for a long time, but in the end I decided to study abroad.

items.explain: つもりだ just states an intention without stressing the moment of decision, and you might not end up going; ことにした often carries a sense of “finally deciding after hesitation” (迷ったけど, いろいろ考えて).

groups.note: Both come from 「どう」 (how) — asking what someone thinks: how about this thing = recommending; how about doing it = suggesting

items.diff: noun + はどうですか recommends a thing; verb ta-form + らどうですか suggests someone do something.

this.tr: If you have a cold, how about this medicine?

that.tr: If you have a cold, why don't you take some medicine?

items.explain: Look at what comes before 「どう」: noun + は (この薬は) → offering a thing for the listener to evaluate or accept; verb ta-form + ら (飲んだら) → urging the listener to take action, which can sound preachy to a superior.

groups.note: Both can be used to urge or suggest

items.diff: はいかがですか offers something and asks if the listener wants it; ませんか invites the listener to do something together.

this.tr: Would you care for some coffee?

that.tr: Would you like to have a coffee together?

items.explain: Look at what comes before: noun + は → just recommending something to the listener, not necessarily drinking it yourself; verb masu-stem + ませんか, often with 「一緒に」 → inviting the listener to do it with you.

groups.note: Both can describe “how a certain part of something is”

items.diff: 象は鼻が長い talks about a feature of “elephants”; 象の鼻は長い just talks about “an elephant's trunk”.

this.tr: Elephants have long trunks.

that.tr: An elephant's trunk is long.

items.explain: Look at what comes before 「は」: 「象は」 → the whole sentence introduces elephants, and 「鼻が長い」 is their feature; 「象の鼻は」 → the topic is just the trunk. To describe features of people or animals, or bodily sensations (田中さんは目が大きい, 私は頭が痛い), use は〜が.

groups.note: Both use 「ある／いる」 for existence — the difference is whether they answer “where is it?” or “what is there?”

items.diff: Nは〜にある answers “where is N?”; 〜にNがある answers “what is there?”.

this.tr: The key is on the desk.

that.tr: There's a key on the desk.

items.explain: Look at which part is new information: asking where something already known (my key) is → 鍵は机の上にあります, with the question 「鍵はどこにありますか」; describing what's in a place → 机の上に鍵があります, with the question 「机の上に何がありますか」.

groups.note: Both は and が can follow the subject

items.diff: は presents a known topic, with the focus on what follows; が puts the focus on the noun before it, answering “who / which”.

this.tr: Nice to meet you. I'm Tanaka.

that.tr: Which one of you is Mr. Tanaka? — I'm Tanaka.

wrong.why: When a question word is the subject, it takes が

items.explain: Look at what's being asked: setting up “I” as the topic and then explaining → は; when asked “who is Tanaka?”, the answer is the noun “I” itself → が. When a question word (誰, 何, どれ) is the subject, it must also take が.

groups.note: Both come from 「より」 — originally “from…”: measuring from B = comparison; from a certain time or place = starting point

items.diff: より followed by an adjective means “than”; after a time or place, followed by 「始まる・出発する」, it's a formal “from”.

this.tr: Tokyo is bigger than Osaka.

that.tr: The meeting will begin at 2 p.m.

items.explain: Look at what follows より: an adjective (大きい, 速い) → the standard of comparison; actions like 「始まります」「出発します」 → the starting point in time or place, a more formal 「から」, common in notices and announcements.

groups.note: All are used to compare two things

items.diff: AはBより〜 narrates with A as the topic; BよりAのほうが〜 focuses on the winner A, and is mostly used to answer “which is more…”.

this.tr: Trains are faster than buses.

that.tr: Which is faster, the train or the bus? — The train is faster than the bus.

items.explain: When simply describing something, use 「AはBより〜」; when asked 「どちらが」, answer with 「〜のほうが」 to put the chosen side in focus. Note that what comes before より is the side that loses.

items.diff: より is the affirmative “more… than…”; ほど〜ない is the negative “not as… as…”.

this.tr: Today is colder than yesterday.

that.tr: Today isn't as cold as yesterday.

items.explain: Look at the end of the sentence: affirmative (寒い) → より; negative (寒くない) → ほど, meaning “doesn't reach B's level”. ほど must always be followed by a negative.

groups.note: Both come from 「ください」 — the imperative of 「くださる」 (to give me)

items.diff: noun + をください asks someone to “give” something; te-form + ください asks someone to “do” something.

this.tr: Excuse me, water, please.

that.tr: Excuse me, could you bring me a glass of water?

items.explain: Look at what comes before ください: noun + を (水を) → asking someone to give you that thing; a verb's te-form (持ってきて) → asking someone to do that action.

groups.note: Both can be used to ask someone for something

items.diff: をください is only for asking for things; をお願いします is more polite and can also be used for services.

this.tr: Excuse me, water, please.

that.tr: Hello, I'd like to check in, please.

wrong.why: チェックイン is a service, not something that can be handed over

items.explain: Look at what you're asking for: things you can hold (水, 切符) → both をください and をお願いします work, the latter being more polite; services like checking in or asking for an explanation → only をお願いします.

items.diff: がほしい just says what you want; をください asks someone for it face to face.

this.tr: Excuse me, could I have the menu?

that.tr: I'm so thirsty. I want some cold water.

items.explain: がほしい states your own wish, can be said to yourself, and isn't necessarily directed at anyone; asking someone in a shop to hand you something → をください. Saying 「メニューがほしいです」 to staff sounds unnatural.

groups.note: Both can mark the target of an action, liking or ability — in English they all look like “objects”, but Japanese splits them into を and が

items.diff: The target of an action takes を; the target of adjectives like 好き・上手 takes が.

this.tr: My sister plays the piano every day.

that.tr: My sister is good at the piano.

wrong.why: 上手 is an adjective, so its target takes が

items.explain: Look at the word at the end: verbs like 弾く, 食べる → を; 好き, 嫌い, 上手, 下手 are adjectives → their target takes が. In English, “like music” or “play the piano well” look like verb + object, so it's tempting to use を.

items.diff: The target of actions like studying or speaking takes を; わかる・できる express ability or a state, and their target takes が.

this.tr: I study Japanese every day.

that.tr: I understand a little Japanese.

items.explain: Look at the verb: 勉強する and 話す are actions you actively do → を; わかる and できる describe an ability or state → が. English “understand Japanese” or “can play tennis” take an object, but Japanese says 「日本語がわかる」「テニスができる」.

groups.note: Both are used to make polite requests

items.diff: をお願いします is more polite and can also be used for services; をください is only for asking for things.

this.tr: Hello, I'd like to check in, please.

that.tr: Excuse me, water, please.

wrong.why: チェックイン is a service, not something that can be handed over

items.explain: Look at what you're asking for: services like checking in, asking for an explanation, or asking for someone on the phone → only をお願いします; things you can hold (水, 切符) → both work, with をお願いします more polite.

items.diff: をお願いします follows a noun and is concise and polite; ていただけませんか follows a verb and makes the request as a question, which is softer.

this.tr: Could you please check this document?

that.tr: Sorry to bother you when you're busy, but would you mind checking this document?

items.explain: Look at what comes before: a noun (確認, 説明) + をお願いします is concise and polite, and very common at work; verb te-form + いただけませんか leaves the decision to the listener with a question, and suits asking for extra help or addressing someone of high status.

groups.note: Both come from 「何（なに）」 — など = なにと, なんか = なにか, meaning “… and the like”

items.diff: The など in や〜など gives neutral examples; なんか after a person or thing often carries contempt or self-deprecation.

this.tr: I prepared tea, sweets and so on.

that.tr: Someone like me could never do it.

items.explain: Look at what comes before など／なんか: several things listed together → just “and so on”; a single person or thing, usually followed by a negative or a poor evaluation (無理だ, 嫌いだ) → “the likes of…, not worth mentioning”, showing contempt or modesty.

groups.note: All are used for listing

items.title: 〜と (listing)
items.diff: や〜など only gives a few examples, implying there are others; と lists everything.

this.tr: There are books, notebooks and so on in my bag.

that.tr: There's a book and a notebook in my bag (just those two).

items.explain: The two sentences differ only in the particle: や (often with など) just picks a few representatives, and there are other things in the bag; what と lists is everything.

items.diff: や〜など lists nouns; たり〜たりする lists actions.

this.tr: I bought clothes, shoes and so on at the department store.

that.tr: On my days off I do things like watching movies and shopping.

items.explain: Look at what's being listed: nouns (服, 靴) → や〜など; actions (見る, する) → verb ta-form + り, ending with 「する」.

items.diff: や〜など works in both writing and speech and only attaches to nouns; とか〜とか is conversational and can also attach to verbs.

this.tr: There's milk, eggs and so on in the fridge.

that.tr: Hey, is there, like, milk or eggs or anything in the fridge?

items.explain: Look at the tone: in です・ます sentences or writing → や〜など; casual talk among friends → とか〜とか. Also, とか can attach to verbs (掃除するとか), but や can't.

groups.note: Both are sentence-final particles

items.diff: よ tells the listener information they don't know; ね seeks agreement or confirmation about something both know.

this.tr: Put on your coat before you go — it's cold out, you know.

that.tr: It's really cold today, isn't it?

items.explain: Look at whether the listener knows: they're still indoors and don't know it's cold → 外は寒いよ (a reminder); you're both outside shivering → 寒いね (sharing the feeling). Using よ for something both know sounds like you're lecturing.

items.title: 〜なあ (exclamation)
items.diff: よ is always said to the listener; なあ is mostly an exclamation, as if talking to yourself.

this.tr: Look, this flower is beautiful, you know.

that.tr: What a beautiful flower.

items.explain: Look at whether there's a listener: calling someone over to look (ほら), telling them something → よ; exclaiming alone while looking at a flower, with no reply needed → なあ.

groups.note: Both come from 「ほう（方）」 — “that side” of two

items.diff: より〜のほうがいい compares two things and says which is better; ta-form + ほうがいい is advice, “you'd better…”.

this.tr: The train is better than the bus.

that.tr: If you have a fever, you'd better go to bed early.

items.explain: Look at what comes before ほう: noun + の (電車の) together with 「より」 → comparing two things; a verb's ta-form (寝た) → giving advice, often followed by 「よ」.

groups.note: All are used for comparison

items.diff: BよりAのほうが〜 focuses on the winner A, and is mostly used to answer “which is more…”; AはBより〜 narrates with A as the topic.

this.tr: Which is faster, the train or the bus? — The train is faster than the bus.

that.tr: Trains are faster than buses.

items.explain: When asked 「どちらが」, answer with 「〜のほうが」 to put the chosen side in focus; when simply describing something, use 「AはBより〜」. Note that what comes before より is the side that loses.

items.diff: より〜のほうが is used to answer “… is more…”; どちらが is used to ask “which is more…”.

this.tr: I like cats more than dogs.

that.tr: Dogs or cats — which do you like more?

items.explain: When asking, set the two options side by side with 「AとBとどちらが」; when answering, mark the losing side with 「より」 and the winning side with 「のほうが」 — don't answer ✗犬と猫と猫のほうが好きです.

items.diff: より〜のほうが says positively that B comes out ahead; ほど〜ない says negatively that A falls short of B.

this.tr: The train is faster than the bus.

that.tr: The bus isn't as fast as the train.

items.explain: Both sentences say the same thing: より〜のほうが is followed by an affirmative (速い), focusing on the winner; ほど must be followed by a negative (速くない), speaking from the losing side.

items.diff: より〜のほうが compares only two things; for three or more, use 「の中で〜がいちばん」.

this.tr: I like cats more than dogs.

that.tr: Of all animals, I like cats the best.

items.explain: First count what's being compared: only two (犬と猫) → より〜のほうが; many within a range (動物の中で) → の中で〜がいちばん.

groups.note: All pair with a negative to express its degree (not at all / not very / not one bit)

items.diff: Both mean “not at all”; 全然 is conversational, まったく is more formal, used in writing and business.

this.tr: I had no idea about that at all!

that.tr: I was entirely unaware of that matter.

items.explain: Look at the register: casual talk among friends with 「よ」 → 全然; honorific language, business or writing (存じませんでした, 問題ございません) → まったく.

items.diff: 全然〜ない is “not at all”; あまり〜ない is “not very”.

this.tr: I don't understand Japanese at all.

that.tr: I don't understand Japanese very well.

items.explain: The two sentences differ only in the adverb: 全然 means not a bit, and is strong; あまり just means not to a high degree — you still understand some. To be more tactful (say, when commenting on someone's cooking), use あまり.

items.diff: ちっとも also means “not one bit”, often with dissatisfaction; and unlike 全然, it can't be used with an affirmative.

this.tr: Don't worry. It's totally fine.

that.tr: No matter how many times I tell him, my son doesn't study one bit.

wrong.why: ちっとも must always be followed by a negative

items.explain: ちっとも can only be used with negatives, often to complain (ちっとも勉強しない, ちっとも来ない); in casual speech 全然 can also go with an affirmative (全然大丈夫), but it's best avoided in formal settings.
